articles.title: Energy security to keep running the show into 2027 amid market shifts, IEA Chief warns
articles.summary: $3.4 trillion global energy spend: Clean tech outpaces fossil fuels nearly 2-to-1 in 2026. IEA Chief says energy markets will not normalize in 2027.
articles.body: Market Outlooks November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago Energy security to keep running the show into 2027 amid market shifts, IEA Chief warns $3.4 trillion global energy spend: Clean tech outpaces fossil fuels nearly 2-to-1 in 2026. IEA Chief says energy markets will not normalize in 2027. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 5 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: IEA As the energy transition reshapes capital allocation, global energy spending is barreling toward a record $3.4 trillion, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). However, IEA’s Executive Director has warned that markets will not return to normal in 2027, as energy security continues to shake up global markets. With the Middle East conflict exposing severe supply vulnerabilities as shipping transit through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a halt, the crisis has highlighted the critical need to diversify supplies and find new delivery routes. While low-emissions technologies, nuclear, storage, and grid expansions pull in $2.2 trillion, leaving traditional oil, gas, and coal trailing behind, fossil fuel extraction is continuing to command a $1.2 trillion slice of the market. Driven by persistent geopolitical energy shocks, global investments are fuelling a nuclear comeback and a surge in clean infrastructure deployment looking toward 2027. Fatih Birol , IEA’s Executive Director, has warned that markets will not revert to pre-war conditions in 2027. Highlighting persistent supply security risks, high fuel pressures, and a rush toward clean tech and nuclear resilience, the ongoing supply vulnerabilities and diesel and gas constraints across Europe appear to be bringing in a permanent shift in how nations approach energy security and infrastructure investment. The IEA has underlined a four-decade high in nuclear power construction alongside the broader $3.4 trillion investment wave, accelerating the race toward grids, efficiency, and storage. Birol is convinced the Hormuz crisis is leading governments to rethink energy priorities and to seek to diversify partners, trade routes, fuels, and technologies. Given that the global energy crisis will continue to cast a long shadow into 2027, based on IEA leadership’s take on the situation, lingering supply bottlenecks and fractured trade routes are locking in a high-alert era for global energy security. Back in May 2026, the IEA’s ‘ World Energy Investment’ report outlined that the conflict in the Middle East was expected to make energy security a top priority among decision-makers, as its effects were being felt most directly in the Middle East and Asia, which had been the destination for 80-90% of energy exports from Gulf producers. The International Energy Agency said at the time that the conflict was fortifying a shift towards security, trust, and diversity as key considerations when choosing energy projects and partners, alongside costs, prices, and environmental performance. As a result, the IEA anticipated wide-ranging implications for the fuels and technologies that countries prioritize, where they get them from, and how they look to achieve other strategic energy objectives. " Changing perceptions of risk and reliability are expected to spur renewed interest in a range of domestically available energy resources: for key fuel importers, this creates upside for renewables, nuclear and potentially also for coal. Renewable energy resources are widely distributed around the world, and preliminary signs indicate that deployment is picking up in some markets heavily affected by the energy crisis. Moreover, if it prompts a faster pace of electrification, the conflict will bring the Age of Electricity even more clearly into view: electricity-related spending already makes up nearly 60% of all global energy investment. " — The International Energy Agency Related Articles Fossil Energy IEA: Oil & gas decline rates sound the alarm over global energy security risks 5 min read The Paris-based agency’s projections indicated that capital flows to the energy sector were expected to grow to $3.4 trillion in 2026, a 5% rise from 2025, mainly from China, the U.S., and the EU, with the clean energy investment set to grow to $2.2 trillion, almost double that of fossil fuels, as investment in clean energy increases year-on-year by 7% in advanced economies and in China, and 4% in other emerging markets, reflecting regional differences with a shared focus on energy security. The IEA has noted that geopolitical tensions, supply restrictions, and market shocks are impacting the outlook looking into 2027, stressing persistent risks to energy security and fuel supplies, alongside surging costs and heightened demand for power infrastructure resilience, energy storage, and nuclear build-outs, which have hit multi-decade highs with roughly 90 GW under construction. The total energy spending in the U.S. is set to rise by 6%, reaching almost $610 billion, with a nearly fourfold uptick in LNG spending in 2026, and battery storage, geothermal, and nuclear power emerging as investment drivers. The United States is expected to represent nearly half of global LNG export capacity by 2030. The investment in the Latin American region is anticipated to increase to $190 billion in 2026, with fossil fuel supply spending continuing to rise, led by deepwater oil developments in Brazil and Guyana and continued activity in Argentina, Mexico, and Venezuela, and grids remaining a focus sector. Energy investments in the European Union are projected to rise to $440 billion in response to energy security and affordability concerns, supported by diversification and accelerated electrification, with natural gas investment remaining important for security of supply, especially through LNG, with infrastructure investments reaching $17 billion in 2025. Africa’s energy spending is forecast to reach $110 billion in 2026, dominated by fossil fuel spending, with growing interest in power generation, critical minerals, and transport, while upstream investment hit $37 billion in 2025, down from $68 billion in 2016, an 11% drop. Investment remains highly concentrated in Algeria, Angola, Egypt, Nigeria, and Libya, which together account for 70% of investment, even though investment in these countries has fallen from $50 billion in 2016 to $25 billion in 2025. On the other hand, capital allocated to emerging producers such as Mozambique, Namibia, Senegal, and Uganda has grown since 2016. The Middle East is continuing to attract energy investment, with natural gas and low-emissions technologies driving investment trends, but upstream oil and gas spending is projected to decline by around 1% in 2026. Eurasia continues to keep fossil fuels as the primary energy source in the region, while investment in renewables, grids, and electrification is projected to reach $43 billion. While total energy spending remains dominated by oil and gas, at $77 billion, regional fossil fuel investment has fallen markedly from past highs. There is a growing focus on power system reliability, grid expansion, and export resilience in countries such as Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan, which includes major public and foreign-backed projects in solar, wind, storage, hydropower and transmission infrastructure. China’s energy investment priorities are shifting from capacity expansion toward broader system strategy, with grid expansion and green finance underpinning energy transition, based on the IEA’s report. The country’s spending is forecast to hit $945 billion in 2026, with grid investment expected to rise sharply to $140 billion, playing a central role in integrating recent renewable additions, supporting electrification, and strengthening energy security. India’s energy investment is projected to climb to $170 billion, driven by a surge in investment in solar PV and oil refining, as for every dollar invested in fossil-based generation, the country invests three in renewables and nuclear power. Japan and Korea’s investment in dispatchable generation is becoming increasingly important for electricity security, while the region is expanding critical mineral investments to reduce supply chain risks by combining transition-related spending with a strong focus on energy security, with total investment projected to reach $122 billion. Southeast Asia’s energy investment continues to grow, with spending on renewables, grids, and end-use sectors anticipated to jump to $57 billion in 2026, as the region’s electricity demand is increasing 1.5 times faster than the global average, with the momentum building for cross-border electricity trade through the ASEAN Power Grid (APG), with $27 billion needed for cross-border interconnections by 2040. articles.title: TotalEnergies forges pacts with Petronas, Sonangol, and Oil India to slash methane footprint
articles.summary: TotalEnergies has deepened partnerships across Malaysia, Angola, and India to expand advanced methane detection and accelerate emissions cuts.
articles.body: Energy Transition November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago TotalEnergies forges pacts with Petronas, Sonangol, and Oil India to slash methane footprint TotalEnergies has deepened partnerships across Malaysia, Angola, and India to expand advanced methane detection and accelerate emissions cuts. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: TotalEnergies As global pressure mounts to curb greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, France’s energy giant TotalEnergies has revealed a trio of new partnerships across geographies, joining forces with national oil companies (NOCs) in Malaysia, Angola, and India to share its cutting-edge methane-tracking technology and drive toward a near-zero emissions future by 2030. During the meeting of the Oil and Gas Decarbonization Charter (OGDC) member companies in Abu Dhabi, TotalEnergies has highlighted its cooperation with national oil and gas companies to reduce methane emissions through its partnerships with Petronas in Malaysia, Sonangol in Angola, and Oil India Limited (OIL) in India. To this end, the French firm has signed a collaboration agreement with Petronas, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) , and JGC Corporation to contribute to the development of the Southeast Asia Methane Emissions Technology Evaluation Center (SEA METEC), which will be a regional center based in Malaysia and dedicated to evaluating methane emissions measurement and monitoring technologies across Southeast Asia. Related Articles Fossil Energy COP28 brings ‘historic’ action as 50 oil & gas players pen decarbonization charter 7 min read The European giant will support the development of SEA METEC by sharing the expertise gained over more than ten years through its own TotalEnergies Anomalies Detection Initiative (TADI) center, Europe’s only facility dedicated to evaluating methane detection and quantification technologies. SEA METEC is expected to strengthen knowledge sharing and support the harmonization of methane emissions measurement and quantification methodologies, enabling companies to better detect, measure, and ultimately curtail their emissions. Patrick Pouyanné , Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TotalEnergies, commented: “Our cooperation with Petronas in Malaysia, Sonangol in Angola and OIL in India illustrates TotalEnergies’ commitment to the OGDC and the momentum it has created among international and national companies. “I am convinced that by sharing technologies, expertise and best practices, we can accelerate concrete action and contribute to our common ambition of achieving near-zero upstream methane emissions by 2030.” Related Articles Fossil Energy TotalEnergies ups methane detection ante and signs up another firm to its drone-based tech 5 min read TotalEnergies has also inked a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Sonangol to strengthen technical cooperation on methane emissions reduction and decarbonization solutions in Angola. The agreement builds on the experience gained through the AUSEA technology and covers methane emissions detection, measurement, monitoring, and reduction, as well as the sharing of best practices, methodologies, and technical expertise. The two companies are working together to identify concrete solutions to reduce methane emissions and flaring, improve energy efficiency, support facility electrification, and advance carbon management solutions. The cooperation is also covering greenhouse gas emissions reporting, technical training, and knowledge sharing, as well as the exploration of financing opportunities, including potential support from the World Bank’s Global Flaring and Methane Reduction (GFMR) Fund. Related Articles Business & Finance TotalEnergies earmarks annual spend of up to $17 billion over next five years 3 min read Building on a first campaign using TotalEnergies’ AUSEA technology to detect and quantify methane emissions over 20 OIL-operated sites in Assam, Oil India and TotalEnergies are strengthening their collaboration with a second field campaign. The first one-month-long campaign provided OIL with data to support its emissions reporting, while demonstrating AUSEA’s ability to accurately detect and quantify methane emissions across diverse sites and field conditions. A second month-long campaign will extend the use of AUSEA to additional OIL-operated sites, further strengthening the cooperation between the two companies on methane emissions reduction. articles.title: Multi-year US deal brings liquidity boost to New Fortress Energy as Mexican FLNG targets 4Q restart
articles.summary: NFE has sealed a long-term lease for 300 MW of mobile turbines with a U.S. company, while its FLNG in Mexico edges closer to a Q4 resumption.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago Multi-year US deal brings liquidity boost to New Fortress Energy as Mexican FLNG targets 4Q restart NFE has sealed a long-term lease for 300 MW of mobile turbines with a U.S. company, while its FLNG in Mexico edges closer to a Q4 resumption. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Altamira Fast LNG 1 Source: New Fortress Energy U.S. energy infrastructure player New Fortress Energy (NFE) has secured a five-year lease agreement to deploy ten mobile turbines, delivering up to 300 MW, to a U.S. investment-grade partner, a move the company’s Chief Executive Officer (CEO) believes will strengthen the firm's liquidity while capitalizing on surging domestic power demand. New Fortress Energy has agreed to lease ten mobile turbines that can generate up to 300 MW of power to an undisclosed U.S.-based investment-grade company for an initial period of five years. The turbines are expected to be delivered in stages beginning in the fourth quarter of 2026 and finalized in the first quarter of 2027. This transaction is expected to be accretive to NFE’s earnings and enhance its liquidity profile. Wes Edens , Chief Executive Officer of NFE, commented: “We evaluated several opportunities for these turbines, and we believe that partnering with an investment-grade counterparty in the United States best aligned with NFE’s priorities. “It provides the Company significant, high-quality cash flows, puts our assets to work more quickly than alternative uses, and serves the growing demand for power in the USA.” According to New Fortress Energy, its Fast LNG (FLNG) unit, also known as FLNG 1, remains on track to return to service in the fourth quarter of 2026 based on its most recent discussions with the manufacturer of the turbine. The FLNG 1 unit went offline because of a mechanical issue with the facility's gas turbine offshore Altamira. This interrupted operations and reduced exports at Mexico’s facility until repairs are completed. The Fast LNG is made up of three repurposed jack-up rigs off the coast of Altamira. NFE secured the go-ahead from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to export LNG to non-free trade agreement (non-FTA) countries for a term of five years and obtained a loan to build its second installation, FLNG 2, with construction works scheduled to be over in the first half of 2026. articles.title: Germany’s SEFE and Trafigura renew gas deal through 2031
articles.summary: SEFE and Trafigura have sealed a multi-year natural gas supply agreement, boosting annual volumes to 30 TWh through 2031.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago Germany’s SEFE and Trafigura renew gas deal through 2031 SEFE and Trafigura have sealed a multi-year natural gas supply agreement, boosting annual volumes to 30 TWh through 2031. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Trafigura Germany’s Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE) is scaling up its long-term gas procurement by locking in a massive 150 TWh supply agreement with commodities player Trafigura to bolster German and European energy security through late 2031. SEFE has signed a new gas supply contract with Trafigura for 30 TWh of natural gas annually over a five-year period, beginning on November 1, 2026, representing a total volume of 150 TWh. The gas will primarily be sourced from Trafigura’s global portfolio. Frédéric Barnaud , SEFE’s Chief Commercial Officer (CCO), commented: “With this new agreement, we are continuing our successful collaboration with Trafigura, whose global reach and deep market expertise make it an important partner for SEFE. “Such partnerships strengthen our ability to source natural gas from a broad range of origins and reinforce our position as a reliable energy provider for our German and European customers.” The agreement allows the company to qualify for cover under Germany’s United Loan Guarantee Scheme (UFK), which guarantees form part of the German Federal Government’s raw materials strategy and support access to strategically important commodities by protecting financing against commercial and political risks. This deal builds on the duo’s partnership, following seamlessly from an existing four-year contract that expired at the end of October 2026, with annual volumes increasing significantly compared with the previous agreement, which provided for approximately 23 TWh per year, further strengthening SEFE’s diversified procurement portfolio. Igor Marin , Global Head of Gas, Power and Renewables at Trafigura, said: “We are pleased to extend our relationship with SEFE through this new five-year supply agreement. “Trafigura’s global gas portfolio and logistics network allow us to deliver reliable supply into Europe, and we are proud to continue contributing to Germany’s energy security with firm deliveries of gas.” The deal with Trafigura comes shortly after SEFE secured its first Canadian multi-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal to enable supplies from an LNG project being developed on Canada’s northwest coast. articles.title: Piraeus container throughput returns to growth in third quarter
articles.summary: Container throughput at Pier I of the Port of Piraeus returned to growth during the third quarter of 2026, despite remaining significantly lower across the first nine months of the year. Piraeus Port Authority (PPA) said third-quarter throughput at Pier I increased by 0.3%, or 524 TEUs, compared with the same period...
articles.body: Container throughput at Pier I of the Port of Piraeus returned to growth during the third quarter of 2026, despite remaining significantly lower across the first nine months of the year. Piraeus Port Authority (PPA) said third-quarter throughput at Pier I increased by 0.3%, or 524 TEUs, compared with the same period in 2025. This marked the terminal’s first positive quarterly performance of 2026. Volumes improved more strongly during August and September, rising by 11.5%, or 10,161 TEUs. PPA attributed the recovery partly to new container-handling agreements with Piraeus Container Terminal and Pier I’s main customer. The agreements took retroactive effect from July and include revised tariffs and handling volumes. During October, Pier I handled five additional containerships and 7,843 TEUs under the agreement with Piraeus Container Terminal. Nine-month container volumes remain lower Despite the third-quarter recovery, Pier I handled 394,338 TEUs during the first nine months of 2026. This represented a 27.8% decline from 546,399 TEUs in the corresponding period of 2025. Local container volumes fell by 34.1% to 131,799 TEUs. Revenue from Pier I decreased by 26% to €34.8 million, while the segment recorded a pre-tax loss of €3.9 million. In the same period last year, Pier I generated a pre-tax profit of €6.5 million. However, revenue from the concession of Piers II and III increased by 3.2% to €70.7 million. During the third quarter alone, concession revenue rose by 9% compared with the same quarter of 2025. PPA revenue and profit decline PPA’s total revenue decreased by 8.2% to €178.8 million during the first nine months. EBITDA fell by 16.9% to €92.6 million, while profit after tax declined by 21.5% to €59.7 million. In the third quarter, revenue reached €66.9 million, down 7% year on year. Net profit fell by 17% to €24.3 million. PPA invested €126.6 million during the nine-month period, an increase of 84.5% compared with the previous year. The port authority said geopolitical developments in the Middle East affected container demand and trade flows, particularly during the first half of 2026. PPA added that the return of containerships to the Suez Canal was becoming more established during the fourth quarter. The company expects canal transits to increase over the coming months and estimates that traffic could fully recover by May 2027.

articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard has detained the cruise ship MSC Poesia at PortMiami, forcing MSC Cruises to cancel an 11-night Caribbean voyage after the vessel remained in port for two...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Pjotr Mahhonin/CC BY-SA 3.0 The U.S. Coast Guard has detained the cruise ship MSC Poesia at PortMiami, forcing MSC Cruises to cancel an 11-night Caribbean voyage after the vessel remained in port for two days. The Panama-flagged cruise ship was detained Sunday, November 1, during what the Coast Guard described as an expanded examination of the vessel. The ship had been scheduled to depart Miami that afternoon but remained docked with passengers aboard as inspectors reviewed its compliance with maritime regulations. In a statement released Tuesday, the Coast Guard said Sector Miami personnel were verifying the vessel’s compliance with international standards and U.S. regulations. “The Coast Guard is tasked with verifying safe and secure commerce,” the agency said, adding that the Captain of the Port’s priority is protecting passengers, crew, the vessel and the environment. The Coast Guard has not disclosed what prompted the expanded examination or identified any specific deficiencies. It also has not indicated when the ship might be cleared to depart. MSC Cruises confirmed Tuesday that it was canceling the voyage after efforts to resolve the issue proved unsuccessful. “Prior to departure, a regulatory matter arose that required resolution,” MSC Cruises said in a statement reported by NBC News. The company said it was unable to resolve the matter in time for the sailing to proceed. The cruise line said affected passengers would receive full refunds and assistance arranging their journeys home. Guests have also been permitted to remain aboard until noon Thursday, November 5, while making alternative travel arrangements. The canceled itinerary was scheduled to visit Jamaica, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras and Belize before returning to Miami on November 12. The detention raises questions about the nature of the regulatory issue that prevented the ship from sailing. Under the Coast Guard’s port state control program, foreign-flagged vessels calling at U.S. ports are subject to examinations to verify compliance with applicable international conventions and U.S. requirements. Serious deficiencies can result in a vessel being detained until the necessary corrective actions are completed. However, neither the Coast Guard nor MSC Cruises has publicly explained what inspectors discovered aboard MSC Poesia , leaving the reason for the detention unclear. Built in 2008, the 92,627-gross-ton MSC Poesia is part of MSC Cruises’ Musica class. The 294-meter vessel has capacity for 3,223 passengers and approximately 1,039 crew members. The ship underwent a major refurbishment earlier this year, including the addition of MSC’s Yacht Club luxury accommodations and upgrades to its dining and wellness facilities. There has been no indication that the refurbishment is connected to the detention. The ship’s next scheduled voyage is a 10-night Caribbean cruise departing Miami on November 12. MSC Cruises has not announced any changes to that sailing. As of Tuesday, the vessel remained in Miami, with no publicly announced timetable for its release. The rise came amid an “increasingly volatile” operating environment at Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, with “reported projectile strikes, vessel fires and other security incidents” throughout October, CAS said. “In the month of October, we registered 30 attacks, if I remember correctly, which is one of the highest we have,” International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told journalists on Nov. 2. While Iranian aerial attacks continue to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, mine collision incidents also remain a threat to vessels traversing the chokepoint, as “there’s no confirmation that there are not mines in the region,” Dominguez added. “I cannot guarantee that it’s safe. That’s why we are not recommending anyone to go through the Strait of Hormuz, and I keep saying for the ships to stay away from it,” Dominguez said during a press conference. Despite elevated security risks over the month, observed and assumed Hormuz traffic totaled 750 transits in October, up from 749 in September, as VLCC traffic fell to 156 transits in October from 184 the previous month, but the declines in crude tanker transits were more than offset by other vessel classes, according to the CAS report. Bulk carrier traffic climbed to 149 transits, the highest since June, according to CAS. LNG carrier crossings, which fell steeply since Qatar LNG production units suffered damage at the start of the Iran war, also climbed, reaching 32 transits, or their highest since the start of the war. LPG tanker traffic fell month over month to 36 transits from 40 on weaker inbound activity, while outbound movements were steady, CAS reported. Daily crossings over the previous three days totaled 24 transits on Oct. 30, 28 transits on Oct. 31, before easing to 17 crossings on Nov. 1, according to CAS. Prominent outbound crude movements between Oct. 30 and Nov. 1 included Bahri VLCCs Lawhah, Aslaf, Majra and Platinum Shine, as well as Sinokor-operated Jamaica Prosperity, Vietnam Prosperity and Colombia Prosperity, CAS reported. Also crossing outbound were Suezmax tankers Tilos I, Ottoman Equity and Cronus, all of which are carrying Gulf crude to India. Headed inbound the strait were Bahri VLCCs Kassab and Gold Shine, Trafigura-linked Kiku and ADNOC’s Al Adlah, according to CAS assessments. Dynacom-operated Aframax Astypalea also appeared to have entered the Gulf for the first time since March. Three LPG tanker transits were recorded from Oct. 30 through Nov. 1, all outbound, CAS reported. Bahri-operated Gas Aqua exited after loading ammonia at Ras Al Khair, while Iranian-linked VLGC Xavia moved out of the Gulf and later positioned near Sohar ahead of an understood ship-to-ship transfer. The Iran-linked Ocean Unity crossed outbound Nov. 1 after remaining offline since mid-July and appeared to be in ballast, according to CAS, which has noted that “[the tanker’s] cargo status may become clearer as the voyage progresses.” Five vessels assessed to have crossed Hormuz during the three-day period were listed on the Iranian Persian Gulf Strait Authority’s blacklist, according to the authority’s website. The Iranian authority had listed 240 vessels as violating its Strait of Hormuz transit guidelines and previously threatened non-compliant vessels with fines, seizure or confiscation. In the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab traffic rose to 1,196 transits in October from 1,154 in September, while tanker movements were stable at 408 versus 404, CAS reported. Northbound traffic increased to 647 transits, about 54% of the monthly total, from 578 in September. Saudi-linked Bab al-Mandab traffic continued to decline sharply, as observed by CAS, falling to 21 transits in October from 52 in September, according to the report. articles.body: Tanker S&P: A Tale of Two Marketsccording to Signal Ocean data, global seaborne refined product in Hellenic Shipping News 04/11/2026 S hip owners are diverging when it comes to their demand for second tanker ships. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the tanker Sale & Purchase market during September and October 2026 reveals an interesting divergence between vessels offered for sale and those actually changing hands, highlighting differences in investment appetite across vessel segments, age groups and shipbuilding countries. Based on our data of tankers above 10,000 DWT, a total of 371 vessels were advised for sale during the two-month period, compared to 146 recorded transactions. Although these figures do not represent a direct conversion rate between listings and sales, they provide valuable insight into the composition of supply and actual buying activity”. According to Xclusiv, “looking at vessel segments, the contrast becomes particularly evident in the larger crude tanker categories. A total of 22 VLCCs and 28 Suezmaxes changed hands, compared to just 13 and 16 vessels respectively appearing in the for-sale dataset. Combined, these two segments accounted for 34% of all transactions but less than 8% of for sale available tonnage. Meanwhile, the MR2 segment recorded 42 sales against 125 vessels offered for sale, while smaller tankers accounted for another 167 listings but only 20 transactions. This divergence suggests that buying activity is disproportionately concentrated in larger tankers, potentially reflecting stronger earnings expectations and investor confidence in crude transportation”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker The shipbroker added that “the age profile reveals another important distinction. Vessels aged 16–20 years dominate the for-sale market of the last 2 months, with 175 units, representing 47% of available tonnage, followed by 100 vessels aged 21 years and above, accounting for another 27%. Together, these categories represent 74% of advertised vessels, compared to 55% of completed transactions. Conversely, vessels aged 11–15 years represented 23% of sales against just 13% of listings, while the 6–10-year category accounted for 8% of transactions but only 3% of supply. Additionally, five resale transactions were recorded, matching the number of resales for sale. These differences suggest that owners are increasingly seeking opportunities to dispose of ageing assets, while buyers demonstrate comparatively greater interest in younger tonnage”. Meanwhile, “shipbuilding origin adds another dimension to this picture. South Korean-built tankers dominate activity, accounting for 146 advised for sale vessels and 68 transactions, representing approximately 39% and 47% of the respective markets. Interestingly, 121 Korean-built tankers offered for sale are already over 15 years old, compared to 38 among those sold. Particularly notable is the 11–15-year category, where 23 Korean-built vessels changed hands against 22 units out in the market, underlining the strong presence of this age group in actual transactions”. “Chinese-built tankers present a different profile. Of the 118 vessels for sale since 1st of September, 42 were resales or aged up to 10 years, while this group accounted for 24 of the 48 recorded Chinese-built sales. Japan, meanwhile, exhibits a significantly older profile, with 51 of its 56 for sale vessels exceeding 15 years, compared to 17 of its 21 sales. Overall, the figures suggest a tanker S&P market characterised by selective investment rather than uniform buying appetite. While larger crude tankers attract substantial transactional activity, the considerable availability of ageing tonnage highlights owners’ willingness to capitalise on current asset values. The different age profiles across Korean, Chinese and Japanese-built vessels further demonstrate that vessel specifications, age and trading potential remain central to investment decisions. Ultimately, the balance between available tonnage and buyer preferences will be instrumental in shaping secondhand values over the coming months”, Xclusiv concluded. articles.title: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter
articles.summary: As shipping’s fuel landscape becomes more diverse, attention is increasingly turning to the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s latest white paper explores the growing role of gas bunker vessels, technical matters to be aware of, and the challenges and opportunities...
articles.body: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 04/11/2026 A s shipping’s fuel landscape becomes more diverse, attention is increasingly turning to the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s latest white paper explores the growing role of gas bunker vessels, technical matters to be aware of, and the challenges and opportunities associated with supporting LNG today while preparing for the fuels of tomorrow. The maritime industry is entering a period of growing fuel diversity. While much of the discussion focuses on fuels, engines, and regulations, the transition will also depend on the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s new white paper, Gas bunker vessels – Facilitating the transition to alternative fuels, details how gas bunker vessels are becoming a critical part of that infrastructure and analyses the key factors shaping their future development, from market growth and vessel design to safety, operational readiness, and the adoption of emerging fuels such as ammonia. LNG success creates a new supply challenge LNG has become the most widely adopted gaseous marine fuel and the first to achieve large-scale commercial deployment. According to DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform, around 900 LNG-fuelled vessels are now in operation worldwide, excluding LNG carriers. Around 650 additional vessels are expected to join the fleet before 2030, further increasing demand for LNG as a marine fuel. As the LNG-fuelled fleet expands, pressure is growing across the entire bunkering ecosystem. LNG consumption by LNG-fuelled vessels increased by more than 500% between 2020 and 2024, with a further 167% growth expected between 2025 and 2030. The white paper argues that bunkering infrastructure is not keeping pace with this rapid expansion, creating a widening gap between fuel demand and available bunkering capacity. “The LNG bunkering market is well supplied today, but the picture could change significantly as the LNG-fuelled fleet continues to expand,” says Martin Cartwright, Global Business Director, Gas Carriers & FSRUs, DNV Maritime. “Our analysis suggests the global LNG bunker vessel fleet may need to more than double by 2030, with between 165 and 208 vessels potentially required worldwide. Meeting that demand will require coordinated investment across the entire bunkering value chain, not just in the vessels themselves.” Gas bunker vessels emerge as a key link in the alternative fuel value chain The report argues that gas bunker vessels should be viewed as more than fuel delivery assets. As shipping adopts a wider range of fuels, they are becoming a critical link between fuel producers, storage facilities, ports, and vessels, helping ensure alternative fuels can be supplied safely, reliably, and at scale. While gas bunker vessels share many characteristics with conventional gas carriers, their role as fuel suppliers creates a distinct operating profile. Frequent ship-to-ship transfers, interactions with a wide variety of receiving vessels, and the need to operate safely in busy port environments place additional demands on vessel design, operational procedures, safety systems, and crew competence. “As the maritime industry adopts new fuels and technologies, understanding the bunker vessels that support the transition is becoming just as important as understanding the fuels themselves,” says Robert Østraat Kjelstadli, Principal Engineer, DNV Maritime, and co-author of the white paper. “These vessels are a critical part of the infrastructure that connects fuel supply with vessel operations. Safe and reliable fuel delivery depends on dedicated vessel designs, robust procedures, and the ability to operate efficiently across a wide range of ports and vessel types.” Converting existing LNG vessels can accelerate capacity growth Meeting future demand does not necessarily depend on newbuild vessels alone. The white paper highlights the conversion of suitable small-scale LNG carriers into dedicated bunker vessels as a practical way to accelerate capacity growth and support developing bunkering markets. “Many of these vessels already possess the containment, cargo-handling, monitoring, and safety systems required for liquefied gas operations,” says Yury Ilchenko, Principal Engineer and Gas Carrier Specialist at DNV. “However, successful conversion requires more than adding transfer equipment. Owners must consider factors such as vessel compatibility, ship-to-ship transfer arrangements, vapour and pressure management, manoeuvrability, emergency response, and operational readiness to ensure the vessel can safely perform its new role as a bunker vessel.” Bunkering safety must scale with LNG demand As gas bunkering becomes more frequent and geographically widespread, maintaining consistently high standards of safety and operational performance becomes increasingly important. Unlike conventional marine fuels, gaseous fuels introduce additional considerations around cryogenic handling, vapour management, pressure control, transfer operations, and emergency response. The white paper highlights how safety, resilience, and competence must develop alongside infrastructure if the industry is to scale bunkering operations successfully. “Gas bunkering is not simply a matter of moving fuel from one vessel to another,” says Ilchenko. “It requires robust procedures, clear responsibilities, resilient systems, and competent people. As operations become more frequent and take place in more locations around the world, maintaining that discipline becomes increasingly important.” Safe gas bunkering depends on people, procedures, and technology The report stresses that safe and reliable bunkering depends on translating technical and regulatory requirements into consistent day-to-day practices. Structured safety management systems, compatibility assessments, ship-to-ship transfer procedures, emergency response arrangements, and competence development all have an important role to play. “Safe gas bunkering is built on a combination of technology, procedures, and people,” says Cartwright. “Operators that establish strong safety management systems, invest in competence development, and adopt a structured approach to risk management will be best positioned to scale operations safely and reliably as demand continues to grow.” Operational readiness should be considered from the earliest stages of vessel design through to routine bunkering activities. The paper also highlights the value of common operating standards, clear allocation of responsibilities, and the use of industry guidance and checklists to support consistent performance across different ports, vessel types, and operating environments. Today’s LNG bunkering investments could accelerate future fuel adoption While the report focuses primarily on LNG, it also examines the growing role of other gaseous fuels, particularly ammonia. Recent regulatory developments and updated class requirements are helping make dedicated ammonia bunker vessels a practical possibility, while many of the operational principles developed through LNG bunkering remain directly relevant. At the same time, the paper argues that today’s investments in LNG bunkering infrastructure have value beyond LNG alone. The vessels, transfer systems, operational experience, and safety frameworks being developed now can help support future fuel pathways, including biomethane, synthetic methane, and ammonia. While the future fuel mix remains uncertain, the need for safe, reliable, and scalable bunkering infrastructure is not. “The future fuel landscape will undoubtedly be more diverse than it is today,” says Cartwright. “Whatever shape that future takes, safe and efficient fuel supply must keep pace with demand. The infrastructure, expertise, and operational experience being built through LNG bunkering today will help create the foundation for the fuels of tomorrow.” Source: DNV, https://www.dnv.com/expert-story/maritime-impact/why-gas-bunker-vessels-will-be-critical-to-shippings-fuel-transition/ Tops 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

While much of the discussion focuses on fuels, engines, and regulations, the transition will also depend on the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale.
LNG success creates a new supply challenge LNG has become the most widely adopted gaseous marine fuel and the first to achieve large-scale commercial deployment.

articles.body: Panamax vessels lose out in Q3 as shifting grain trade boosts smaller bulk carriers in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 04/11/2026 P anamax bulk carriers have emerged as the principal losers from changing global grain trade patterns, while smaller Supramax and Handysize vessels have benefited from the redistribution of wheat and corn shipments, according to new research from international shipbroker IFCHOR GALBRAITHS (IG). The analysis reveals that Panamax wheat and corn shipping demand fell by 27.65 billion tonne-miles in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the average for the corresponding quarters of 2023–2025. This represents a reduction equivalent to approximately 1.4% of the segment’s total third-quarter dry bulk demand. By contrast, Supramax vessels gained 10.15 billion tonne-miles, equivalent to approximately 0.6% of total segment demand, while Handysize vessels recorded an increase of 1.53 billion tonne-miles, or 0.2%. The contrasting performance reflects a significant reshaping of global grain trade, as reduced Russian and Ukrainian exports, stronger shipments from alternative suppliers and a sharp decline in Brazilian corn exports alter both cargo availability and voyage distances. Alternative suppliers benefit, but Brazil weighs on Panamax demand IG’s research shows that reduced Russian and Ukrainian wheat and corn shipments eliminated 30.63 billion tonne-miles of shipping demand during the quarter. Alternative suppliers, notably Argentina, the United States and Canada, recorded substantial gains. Argentine exports generated an additional 28.72 billion tonne-miles, followed by the US (+17.03 billion) and Canada (+15.81 billion). Argentina’s increased exports were particularly supportive of geared bulk carriers, with Supramax and Handysize vessels benefiting from the changing distribution of cargoes. Increased US shipments, meanwhile, were concentrated in the Panamax segment. However, these gains were heavily outweighed by a sharp contraction in Brazilian grain exports. Brazilian wheat and corn shipments generated 53.19 billion fewer tonne-miles than the historical third-quarter average, reflecting a 33.9% reduction in export volumes and an 18.4% decline in average voyage distances. The weakness of Brazil’s corn export season and growing domestic demand from its expanding corn ethanol industry proved particularly damaging for Panamax demand, offsetting much of the benefit from stronger grain shipments elsewhere. Serena Piazzo, Senior Analyst at IG said: “The changing geography of global grain trade is creating very different conditions for different parts of the dry bulk fleet. “Although disruption to Black Sea exports has encouraged greater reliance on alternative suppliers, particularly in the Americas, the benefits have not been evenly distributed. “Supramax and Handysize vessels have gained from changing cargo flows and longer voyages on certain routes. Panamax vessels, however, have been particularly exposed to weaker Brazilian corn exports and a reduction in average voyage distances. “It demonstrates that the impact of trade disruption on freight markets depends not simply on how far commodities travel, but also on the availability of cargoes and the types of vessels employed.” Overall grain shipping demand contracts Despite increased activity on some alternative trade routes, IG calculates that global wheat and corn shipping demand declined by 15.98 billion tonne-miles, or 3.4%, compared with the historical third-quarter average. The reduction is equivalent to approximately 0.2% of total global dry bulk tonne-mile demand across all commodities. The findings underline how changes in agricultural production, export competitiveness and trading patterns can produce markedly different outcomes across the dry bulk fleet. The research forms part of IFCHOR GALBRAITHS’ wider agricultural commodity analysis, including its Agri 360 service, which examines production forecasts, trade flows and their implications for shipping markets. articles.body: Maritime clusters urged to turn global cooperation into measurable action in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 Maritime clusters must turn international cooperation into practical projects that unlock investment, support innovation and strengthen the industry’s workforce, speakers told the International Association of Maritime Clusters’ (IAMC) inaugural online conference. The Building Bridges conference, held on 2 November under the theme How Diverse Maritime Clusters Can Work Together, attracted more than 200 delegate registrations. Discussions examined how clusters can tackle shared challenges while protecting commercial interests, and why regional maritime communities need a stronger international voice. Opening the conference, IAMC President Peter Shaerf highlighted the pressures created by shifting trade flows, geopolitical uncertainty, decarbonisation and widening skills gaps. “Everything is felt locally. But it can’t necessarily be solved locally,” he said. Speakers stressed that competition for contracts and investment should not prevent clusters from sharing knowledge, training approaches, market intelligence and experience of new technologies. Protecting commercially sensitive information was essential to building the trust needed for that cooperation. Participants emphasised that these proposals should produce benefits for individual member companies. The discussion also exposed barriers to maritime innovation.These included inconsistent regulatory frameworks and difficulties securing finance to take promising technologies beyond pilot projects and into commercial use. Joshua Berger, President and CEO of Maritime Blue, described opportunities for clusters to share access to test facilities and regulatory sandboxes, helping innovators demonstrate solutions in different markets, while Gonçalo Santos from Forum Oceano in Portugal, proposed an exchange between clusters that would connect smaller businesses with testing opportunities and report results within 12 months. Claudia Grant, Deputy Director General of the Maritime Authority of Jamaica, suggested mapping the capabilities of different clusters to make potential partnerships easier to identify. Caribbean cooperation on maritime education and the potential for collaboration on alternative fuels illustrated how neighbouring countries could build on complementary strengths. Peter Shaerf, President of the IAMC The Small Cluster Big Voice session challenged assumptions that influence depends on size. Regional clusters described their ability to connect businesses, researchers and public authorities, mobilise smaller companies and move quickly from an idea to implementation. Stu Baker, CEO of Maritime Solent, emphasised the distinctive perspective regional clusters bring by working across maritime’s entire value chain. Their success, he said, should be judged through the achievements of the businesses and communities they support. Ruth Wood, Chief Executive of Mersey Maritime, stressed that effective cluster structures must reflect local circumstances. “There’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to cluster model,” she said, pointing to the importance of regional specialisms and expertise. Speakers also discussed the need for government engagement alongside credible financial backing from industry. The Talent Without Borders panel placed recruitment, retention and lifelong learning at the centre of maritime’s future. Participants called for clearer pathways between sea and shore, closer links between employers and educators, and greater recognition of people entering maritime from other careers. Matthew Stewart, Deputy Dean of Warsash Maritime School, urged the industry to focus on new talent rather than young talent alone, while Dr Momoko Kitada of the World Maritime University highlighted the need for inclusive workplaces and opportunities for younger people to contribute ideas and be heard. Irene Rosberg, Programme Director at the Copenhagen Business School, said learning must extend throughout an organisation: “But professional development cannot just stop once somebody reaches the shore management or the boardroom.” Columbia Group CEO Andreas Hadjipetrou highlighted the importance of improving seafarers’ living conditions, family connectivity and career development. He also underlined the need to judge cooperation through delivery. “However, the results will have to be measured not by wishful thinking, but by real action,” he said. The session was chaired expertly by Capt Lee Clarke, Managing Director of the Isle of Man Maritime. Practical proposals emerging from the conference included shared testing access, exchanges for smaller businesses and closer training partnerships, with speakers urging participants to turn new contacts into projects whose results could be demonstrated at future meetings. articles.body: Limpet Mines Return to the Gulf as Iran Strikes Four Tankers Near the Strait of Hormuz in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 Between October 29 and 30, Iran attacked at least four tankers across the Strait of Hormuz and the waters around it. The attacks ranged from projectiles to hull-mounted explosives, and they struck laden and empty vessels, Qatari- and UAE-owned tonnage, and tankers that had spent weeks operating dark. Iranian sources separately claimed that four tankers hit mines in the Strait and caught fire, but it is unclear whether they were referring to additional vessels beyond the four confirmed. Projectiles Strike a Laden LNG Carrier Inside the Gulf On October 30, AL MAYEDA (IMO 9397298), a Marshall Islands-flagged, Qatari-owned LNG carrier, laden with an unknown quantity of LNG according to Vortexa, was struck by three projectiles around 18:00 UTC, approximately 40 nautical miles south of Lavan Island. Windward data show AL MAYEDA turning around at 18:33 UTC before going dark at 22:17 UTC. AL MAYEDA had previously been dark between September 27 and October 30, and crossed inbound through the Strait of Hormuz during that period. Limpet Mines Return to the Gulf The same day, a small boat approached LOUISE 1 (IMO 9290323), a Panama-flagged, Panama-owned crude oil tanker, approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, and emplaced two explosive devices on its hull. The explosion caused a fire in the engine room and briefly disabled the vessel. LOUISE 1 was last reported laden with 1.02 million barrels of crude on September 28, according to Vortexa, at its last AIS-reported position 12 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan. It has not reported a position since. Dark Shuttle Tankers Come Under Fire Two more tankers were hit while likely transiting the Strait dark. RITI (IMO 9249075), a Panama-flagged, Marshall Islands-owned crude oil tanker in ballast, according to Vortexa, was attacked in the Strait on October 30, likely during a dark inbound transit, and caught fire. Oman evacuated 25 crew members from the vessel 1.6 nautical miles off the Musandam Peninsula. RITI’s last known AIS position was on October 29, approximately 36 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan. NASA FIRMS imagery did not detect a thermal anomaly off Musandam during this period, likely indicating the fire was extinguished. On October 29, ARZANAH (IMO 9928023), a Liberia-flagged, UAE-owned crude oil tanker, was targeted while transiting an undisclosed part of the Strait. Vortexa last reported it laden with 2.14 million barrels of crude on October 17, and it has been dark since that date. Why the Return of Limpet Mines Matters This latest round of attacks continues the trend established this month while expanding the methods Iran is using. Limpet mines are a cost-effective weapon against tankers. They were last successfully used in the region in 2019, when multiple tankers were targeted at anchorages in the Gulf of Oman. The shift matters because it widens the threat beyond projectiles. A small boat that can approach a tanker and place explosives on its hull turns any slow-moving or anchored vessel into a potential target, including the dark shuttle tankers that rely on staying off AIS to avoid detection. This threat is particularly acute inside the Strait, where the ability to maneuver is already limited and small boats are regularly moving inside the waterway. Transits Are Still Rising The attacks, along with ongoing rhetoric about a possible resumption of combat operations in the Middle East, have not reduced Strait of Hormuz transits. Between October 30 and the morning of November 1, there were approximately 24 AIS-visible transits, compared with 18 AIS-visible transits in the same window between October 28 and 30. Shipowners continue to show a willingness to transit the Strait despite almost daily attacks from Iran. This very likely reflects the attraction of high freight rates for operators willing to take on the risk, and the continued push by Gulf States to move oil through the STS shuttle. Outlook That willingness has a limit. Should combat operations resume at a level of intensity similar to the first week of March, transits, already modest, would be expected to fall to near zero within the first 72 hours of the conflict as shipowners reassess the risk of exposure in the Strait. Source: Windward 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The attacks ranged from projectiles to hull-mounted explosives, and they struck laden and empty vessels, Qatari- and UAE-owned tonnage, and tankers that had spent weeks operating dark.
Iranian sources separately claimed that four tankers hit mines in the Strait and caught fire, but it is unclear whether they were referring to additional vessels beyond the four confirmed.
Windward data show AL MAYEDA turning around at 18:33 UTC before going dark at 22:17 UTC.

articles.title: Chinese Penetrate South Korea’s LNG Carrier Market
articles.summary: Chinese shipbuilders secured approximately 40% of all newly ordered large liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers worldwide during the first to third quarters of this year, January to September. While China leads in the general merchant ship market, such as container ships and bulk carriers, by leveraging price...
articles.body: Chinese Penetrate South Korea’s LNG Carrier Market in Shipbuilding News 04/11/2026 Chinese shipbuilders secured approximately 40% of all newly ordered large liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers worldwide during the first to third quarters of this year, January to September. While China leads in the general merchant ship market, such as container ships and bulk carriers, by leveraging price competitiveness, large high-value-added LNG carriers with a capacity of 174,000 cubic meters or more were considered a market dominated by South Korean shipbuilders, who possess differentiated technology. Chinese shipyards have aggressively penetrated this sector this year. According to Clarksons Research, a British shipbuilding and shipping analysis institution, as of the third quarter of this year, South Korea has accumulated 173 orders, while China has 71, maintaining a significant gap. However, this year, a clear trend has emerged where China has rapidly strengthened its LNG carrier production capabilities over recent years and is closing the gap at a rapid pace. While the shipbuilding industry notes, “LNG carriers, which remain more profitable, are still ordered from South Korean shipyards,” there is growing tension that complacency could lead to being overtaken. ◇China Overcoming the Gap Through Production Capacity LNG carriers transport gas liquefied at minus 163 degrees Celsius, making cargo containment technology crucial. Key aspects include ensuring airtightness to prevent gas leakage and reliquefaction. While French company GTT virtually monopolizes cargo containment technology, South Korean shipyards with long experience are highly regarded for their welding, construction, and operational technologies that enhance fuel efficiency. Particularly, LNG carriers are difficult to order based solely on price competitiveness, as any issues with the vessel can lead to significant losses. However, Chinese shipyards have recently entered the LNG carrier market one after another, beginning to accumulate experience and engaging in a “long-term battle.” Until 2021, only Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding in China could construct large LNG carriers. As the first Chinese company to build and deliver a large LNG carrier in 2008, it grew by securing 36 orders out of 128 LNG carriers ordered by Qatar during its mass LNG production drive from 2020 to 2024, excluding those secured by South Korean shipyards. By 2025, Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding increased its annual construction capacity from three to 11 vessels by establishing a dedicated LNG carrier dock. Over the past four years, four additional Chinese shipyards—Jiangnan Shipyard, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry, Yangzijiang Shipyard, and China Merchants—have entered the LNG carrier market. Jiangnan Shipyard delivered its first 175,000 cubic meter-class LNG carrier to a shipowner in November 2024, while Dalian Shipyard did so in September of last year, already accumulating shipbuilding experience. In September, Chinese shipyard Hengli Petrochemical announced an aggressive market entry plan, constructing two large LNG carriers before securing shipowners and selling them through a “build-first, sell-later” approach. Another factor is that South Korea’s “Big Three” shipbuilders—HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, and Samsung Heavy Industries—have virtually saturated their docks capable of constructing large LNG carriers. Chinese shipyards are capitalizing on this by securing orders from shipowners urgently needing LNG carriers amid the global energy transition. ◇The Battle of Technological Prowess Begins Now South Korea’s shipbuilding industry sees the next three to four years as a critical period. LNG carriers typically undergo special inspections every five years to check their cargo tanks and major equipment. Except for Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding, China’s newer shipbuilders have only recently begun delivering large LNG carriers, leaving their quality and reliability unproven through these inspections. Their vessels are expected to undergo the checks around 2029-2030, when their operational reliability will be assessed. Many in the industry fear that fierce competition will begin in earnest if Chinese shipbuilders win shipowners’ trust at that point. “Now is our golden window while we still have the lead,” a shipbuilding industry official said. “We urgently need to advance our technology further to widen the gap.” Source: Chosun Daily 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

However, this year, a clear trend has emerged where China has rapidly strengthened its LNG carrier production capabilities over recent years and is closing the gap at a rapid pace.

articles.title: India’s crude imports hit record high in Oct as refiners stock up for festivals, product exports
articles.summary: Crude imports by Indian refiners rose to an all-time high of 5.54 million b/d in October, as refiners capitalized on improved availability to build supplies ahead of festival demand, while processing higher volumes to produce additional middle distillates for international markets facing supply tightness, industry...
articles.body: India’s crude imports hit record high in Oct as refiners stock up for festivals, product exports in Freight News 04/11/2026 Crude imports by Indian refiners rose to an all-time high of 5.54 million b/d in October, as refiners capitalized on improved availability to build supplies ahead of festival demand, while processing higher volumes to produce additional middle distillates for international markets facing supply tightness, industry sources and analysts said Nov. 3. Domestic-bound crude imports in October were up 9% from both September and the same month a year earlier, according to data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab). The monthly average surpassed the previous high of 5.50 million b/d imported in March 2025. “Russian imports have come off the peaks we saw in June and July, but they’re still close to 2 million b/d in October. At the same time, we are seeing more barrels coming out of the Middle East, particularly from Saudi Arabia and Iraq, and Indian refiners are taking advantage of that availability ahead of stronger seasonal demand,” said Premasish Das, executive director for oil analytics at S&P Global Energy CERA. Russian crude shipments to India rose sharply in the first half of 2026, increasing from 1.17 million barrels/day in January to a peak of 2.43 million b/d in June, according to CAS. Flows eased to 2.05 million b/d in July, 1.98 million b/d in August, and 1.64 million b/d in September, but picked up to nearly 2.1 million b/d in October. “An Oct. 16 US waiver reduced the immediate risk of additional measures affecting buyers of Russian crude. However, the waiver has no specified expiry and remains revocable, while existing Russia-related sanctions continue to leave importers exposed to renewed policy pressure,” said Saransh Katiyar, liquid bulk analyst at CAS. US President Donald Trump signed an executive order Oct. 16, waiving measures included in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act for the largest buyers of Russian oil, citing “national interests,” days before they were due to take effect. The legislation targeted buyers of Russian hydrocarbons, allowing the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas by total volume over the year before enactment, among other measures. Countries such as India can continue to import Russian crude without immediately facing additional US penalties or tariffs. However, the waiver does not permanently revoke the law, and it can be withdrawn. As a result, buyers may choose to diversify their oil supplies and remain cautious about future sanctions risks, refining sources said. Freight economics CERA’s Das added that the economics of Russian barrels were changing as freight costs remain high. Uncertainty around US concessions on Russian oil, the impact of drone attacks on Russian refining, and competition from Chinese buyers also mean Indian refiners will continue to look for opportunities across different sources of supply, depending on availability and relative attractiveness. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, last assessed Dirty Black Sea to West Coast India freight at a lumpsum of $28 million on Oct. 30, nearly double the year-to-date average of $14.5 million. Analysts said the increase in October crude imports for Indian refiners was also supported by higher arrivals from Angola and the US. “Favorable transatlantic arbitrage economics encouraged additional US crude flows into India, while stronger liftings of Angolan heavy-sweet and medium-sour grades also contributed to the rise,” Katiyar said. US crude flows in 2026 averaged 125,000 b/d over January-October, with inflows reaching 150,000 b/d in October, up 16% from September levels, CAS data showed. In addition, Middle Eastern producers were making a clear effort to regain market share, giving Indian refiners a wider range of supply options and contributing to the increase in overall imports, Das said, adding that India’s crude imports were likely to remain elevated, supported by strong refining margins and the start-up of new capacity. Improving availability “Indian refiners are swiftly capitalizing on improved crude availability to maximize utilization rates and secure more cargoes to meet both festive demand at home and export more volumes to deficit markets,” said B. Anand, former CEO of Nayara Energy and founder of consultancy firm Meridian Partners. Indian refineries processed 5.62 million b/d in September, the oil ministry’s provisional estimates showed, reflecting 9.1% higher processing from a year earlier as imports by the world’s third-largest buyer rose despite supply concerns due to the Middle East conflict. The crude processed in September was 6.6% higher than the month’s target of 5.27 million b/d, it said. The processed volume in September was 2.7% higher than 5.47 million b/d in August, the ministry said. Analysts said India’s increase in crude imports in October may partly reflect a buildup of delayed cargoes rather than a sustained change in buying patterns. The movement of crude through the Strait of Hormuz, which remained partially open, also affected the timing and routing of shipments, they added. “While the headline number on India’s crude imports looks impressive, it is still not business as usual and can be a factor of supplies being bunched and refiners looking at stocking up available barrels,” said Rajat Kapoor, managing director for oil and gas at Synergy Consulting. “Refiners have been buying any cargo they can find in order to run plants above nameplate capacity and keep the domestic market supplied ahead of the Diwali festival season,” he said. India’s total seaborne crude discharges, including volumes transferred ship-to-ship and subsequently redistributed to other markets, rose 19% month over month to 6.4 million b/d in October, CAS data showed. Source: Platts 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook
articles.summary: Singapore and Malaysia Bunker fuel availability remains tight in Singapore, with delayed cargo arrivals and congestion at loading terminals continuing to constrain supply, a source said. articles.body: ENGINE: East of Suez Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 Singapore and Malaysia Bunker fuel availability remains tight in Singapore, with delayed cargo arrivals and congestion at loading terminals continuing to constrain supply, a source said. VLSFO lead times are currently around 13-15 days. Last week, suppliers recommended lead times ranging from around 13 days at the earliest to more than three weeks. HSFO lead times have also settled at 13-15 days, compared with a range of around 13 days to as long as three weeks previously. LSMGO lead times have eased slightly to 8-10 days from 9-11 days last week. In Malaysia, bunker supply remains constrained across several fuel grades at Port Klang. Prompt VLSFO availability is particularly tight, while LSMGO supplies remain limited and HSFO availability continues to face pressure. East Asia VLSFO and HSFO availability remains tight in Zhoushan, despite subdued demand. Lead times for both grades have increased to around 15 days, from 12 days last week. Low inventories and adverse weather have restricted supply, while customs formalities have further delayed delivery schedules, a source said. In contrast, LSMGO availability in Zhoushan is good, with lead times falling to two days from four days a week earlier. Supply conditions remain uneven across other Chinese ports. Dalian and Qingdao have sufficient VLSFO and LSMGO stocks, although HSFO availability remains tight in Qingdao. Tianjin is facing shortages across all three major fuel grades, while supplies of VLSFO and HSFO remain limited in Shanghai. LSMGO availability in Shanghai is relatively stable. Supply constraints also persist in southern China. Suppliers in Fuzhou, Xiamen, Yangpu and Guangzhou are reporting shortages of VLSFO and LSMGO. Hong Kong’s bunker market remains stable, with suppliers recommending lead times of around seven days for the major fuel grades. In Taiwan, VLSFO and LSMGO deliveries can be arranged within two days at Keelung, Hualien, Kaohsiung and Taichung, largely unchanged from the previous week. Bunker demand has picked up across South Korea as declining Brent futures have brought benchmark prices lower. Busan’s VLSFO price has dropped by around $80/mt since the end of October to approximately $1,390/mt, according to a South Korean trader. At southern ports, including Busan, Ulsan, Masan, Onsan, Yeosu and Kwangyang, lead times for all major fuel grades are currently around 4-9 days, compared with 5-8 days a week earlier. Availability has also improved at western ports, including Incheon, Daesan, Dangjin, Pyeongtaek and Taean. Lead times for VLSFO, LSMGO and HSFO at these ports have fallen to 4-9 days from 5-8 days previously. However, adverse weather could disrupt bunker operations at several South Korean ports in the coming days. Busan and Ulsan may experience interruptions on 6-7 November, while operations at Yeosu and Daesan could be affected between 5 and 7 November. VLSFO and HSFO availability remains severely constrained at several Japanese ports, including Tokyo, Chiba and Kawasaki, where suppliers recommend lead times of around 9-13 days. Supplies of both grades are also tight in Nagoya, Yokkaichi, Osaka, Kobe, Mizushima, Tokuyama and Oita. Most offers at these ports are subject to enquiry. Kashima is also experiencing tight availability of VLSFO and HSFO. Oceania Bunker fuel availability remains stable in Western Australia, with VLSFO readily available at Kwinana and Fremantle. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around seven days. Each port has only one supplier, and all bunker deliveries are carried out by barge. Supply conditions remain mixed along Australia’s east coast. Port Kembla has normal VLSFO availability, with deliveries possible by truck or pipeline. Sydney has sufficient stocks of VLSFO and LSMGO, although HSFO availability is tighter, with suppliers generally requiring around seven days’ notice. Brisbane and Gladstone have ample VLSFO and LSMGO supplies, with lead times of approximately one week. Meanwhile, VLSFO availability has improved in Melbourne and Geelong. HSFO availability, however, has tightened further in Melbourne and Brisbane. In Western Australia, pipeline bunkering at Dampier Cargo Wharf (DCW) is expected to remain suspended for another three weeks. Deliveries are currently possible only by truck, an Australia-based source said. The approaching cyclone season could introduce further risks to bunker operations across Australia, a source said. Running from November to April, the season could disrupt fuel availability at ports nationwide. New Zealand’s bunker market remains broadly stable, with VLSFO readily available at Tauranga and Auckland. Suppliers at both ports recommend lead times of around four days. At Marsden Point, vessels can receive VLSFO and LSMGO directly through the pipeline. Adverse weather remains the primary operational risk in New Zealand, particularly in Wellington and ports across the South Island, where disruptions to marine operations could delay bunker deliveries. In Papua New Guinea, LSMGO availability remains tight at Rabaul, Madang and Lae. South Asia Suppliers recommend bunker lead times of around 3-4 days for all three major fuel grades at several key Indian ports, including Mumbai, Cochin, Paradip, Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Haldia, Chennai, Tuticorin and New Mangalore, according to an India-based source. High waves are forecast at Visakhapatnam port from 3 November, potentially disrupting bunker operations and delaying deliveries. In Sri Lanka, lead times for all major fuel grades remain around three days at both Colombo and Hambantota. Middle East VLSFO availability in Fujairah has improved despite continued disruption to vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz amid US-Iran tensions, a regional source said. However, supplies of LSMGO and HSFO remain limited. In Saudi Arabia, bunker demand has eased slightly, while fuel availability and delivery schedules continue to vary across ports. Jeddah generally has stable LSMGO supplies, although VLSFO availability remains tight. Bunker activity at Omani ports has remained steady, with demand and supply conditions largely unchanged from the previous month. Vessel activity is particularly high at Duqm, which could affect delivery schedules. LSMGO deliveries can generally be arranged within 2-3 days at Omani ports, including Salalah, Sohar, Duqm and Muscat. Actual lead times depend on the port, required quantity and terminal approvals, an Oman-based trader said. “Supply at Qatar’s Ras Laffan is restricted, and Egypt’s Port Suez is also facing low bunker inventories,” a Middle East-based source said. Djibouti, meanwhile, continues to face limited availability across the major fuel grades. Source: By Tuhin Roy, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Haparanda–Gothenburg rail service opens an export corridor
articles.summary: A new rail connection between Haparanda and the Port of Gothenburg will launch on 5 November, giving Finnish and northern Swedish industry a way to consolidate cargo in Haparanda before onward transport to global markets. articles.body: A new rail connection between Haparanda and the Port of Gothenburg will launch on 5 November, giving Finnish and northern Swedish industry a way to consolidate cargo in Haparanda before onward transport to global markets. For cargo moving from Oulu to Asia, the solution is expected to cut transit time by eight days compared with traditional transport routes. Haparanda’s position on the Swedish-Finnish border makes it well suited to gathering cargo from both countries, and the stated ambition is to develop it into a cross-border logistics hub with a direct rail link to Gothenburg. Through APM Terminals Gothenburg, the service connects into international shipping networks, including direct links to Asia. The route allows larger volumes to travel by rail, making better use of Sweden’s existing railway infrastructure, and offers northern industry added capacity and a dependable year-round option, including in winter when ice in the Gulf of Bothnia can disrupt shipping. Mathias Weismann Poulsen, Head of Commercial at APM Terminals Gothenburg, said Haparanda has significant potential as a cross-border inland hub and described the initiative as an example of connecting the Nordic region to Gothenburg by rail where demand exists, helping Nordic industry reach global markets efficiently and competitively. Roger Danell, Municipal Director of the City of Haparanda, said the project shows how existing infrastructure can create a new, sustainable export corridor, and called it a first step toward a strategic green export corridor between the Gulf of Bothnia and Sweden’s west coast.

articles.title: Wärtsilä completes methane reduction upgrades on three Chevron LNG carriers
articles.summary: Wärtsilä has completed engine conversions on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation, marking the first phase of a project aimed at reducing methane emissions from LNG-powered vessels. The work involved converting one Wärtsilä 50DF engine on each vessel from dual-fuel operation to spark gas...
articles.body: Wärtsilä has completed engine conversions on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation, marking the first phase of a project aimed at reducing methane emissions from LNG-powered vessels. The work involved converting one Wärtsilä 50DF engine on each vessel from dual-fuel operation to spark gas technology. The modification is designed to reduce methane slip, which occurs when unburned methane escapes during engine operation. Following the completion of these three conversions, Wärtsilä and Chevron plan to carry out similar upgrades on three additional LNG carriers during the remainder of 2026 and in 2027. The programme will cover six vessels once all planned conversions are completed. Spark gas technology targets methane emissions The conversion replaces diesel pilot fuel ignition with spark ignition. This allows the engine to use a different combustion process, which is designed to improve efficiency and reduce unburned methane emissions. The technology uses an electrically controlled pre-combustion chamber valve to support more efficient combustion. According to Wärtsilä, the conversion is expected to reduce methane slip to approximately 1.1% of fuel use, based on the International Maritime Organization’s weighted E2 test cycle. However, this figure represents an estimated performance level rather than a published measurement from the three converted vessels. Barbara Pickering, President of Chevron Shipping, said the project would provide operational insights into technologies designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from LNG-fuelled ships. Meanwhile, Roger Holm, President of Wärtsilä Marine, highlighted the role of cooperation between technology providers and shipping companies in developing lower-emission solutions. Further LNG carrier conversions planned The project builds on an earlier agreement between Wärtsilä and Chevron to evaluate and implement methane reduction technology across the LNG carrier fleet. The spark gas conversion solution is also available to other vessel operators using Wärtsilä 50DF engines with diesel-electric propulsion. According to Wärtsilä, most vessels equipped with this engine configuration are LNG carriers. With the first three conversions now completed, the remaining work will extend the project to six vessels. The initiative forms part of wider industry efforts to address methane slip, an important environmental concern associated with LNG-powered shipping.
