articles.title: Longer Navy Deployments Demand More Than Tough Sailors
articles.summary: By Chris Servello (OpEd) Ten and eleven month Navy deployments may become the norm for the next couple of years. That’s the message Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle and Master Chief...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman talk with U.S. Sailors during an all-hands call at Naval Air Station Sigonella, Sicily, Italy, Oct. 5, 2026. (U.S. Navy photo by Joey Rolfe) By Chris Servello (OpEd) Ten and eleven month Navy deployments may become the norm for the next couple of years. That’s the message Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON) John Perryman delivered this past week. It’s not particularly good news, but it’s news that Sailors and their families deserve to hear. Credit to both leaders for being upfront about it. For years, the Navy has struggled to meet growing operational demands with too few ships . Deployments get extended , maintenance schedules slip and crews spend more time away from home than anyone originally planned. None of this is new, but hearing the Navy’s senior leadership acknowledge that longer deployments may be the standard rather than the exception is important. As MCPON Perryman pointed out, uncertainty is often what makes these deployments especially hard. A family can prepare for ten months apart. It’s much harder to prepare for seven months that becomes eight, then nine, then ten, with each extension arriving just as homecoming seems within reach. Admiral Caudle is also right that the lasting solution is a bigger Navy with more capacity and flexibility. We’ve needed that for years, and the urgency has only grown. But building ships takes time. So does expanding shipyard capacity, working through maintenance backlogs and growing the number of qualified Sailors. Even if the Navy makes all the right decisions today, meaningful relief is years away. That leaves an immediate question: What can the Navy do right now to make this new deployment reality more manageable? Retired Admiral Bill Moran , who served as Chief of Naval Personnel and later Vice Chief of Naval Operations, used to emphasize three principles when discussing how the Navy should manage its people: Trust, Balance and Stability. It’s a pretty good way to think about what needs to happen next. Trust begins with being straight with people, especially when the news isn’t good. If a deployment is likely to last ten or eleven months, say so. Don’t build expectations around seven months when everyone knows there’s a good chance the ship will be extended. And when plans change, explain why as soon as operational security allows. Families make real decisions based on deployment schedules. Childcare, jobs, finances, school calendars and family obligations all depend on knowing when someone will be home. Repeated extensions make an already difficult situation considerably worse. Of course, the Navy can’t predict every crisis or operational requirement. Nobody expects it to. But there’s a difference between uncertainty that comes with military operations and uncertainty created by poor communication. Trust also means listening. Navy families know where support systems work and where they don’t. Commanding officers and senior enlisted leaders should have the flexibility to address those problems without turning every reasonable request into a bureaucratic exercise. Nobody joins the Navy expecting an easy life. Long deployments, missed birthdays, holidays and anniversaries come with the profession. Sailors understand that, and their families generally do too. But accepting sacrifice doesn’t mean the Navy gets a pass on making life harder than it needs to be. If ten and eleven month deployments become routine, the Navy should be looking at everything within its authority to offset the additional burden. At sea, that means protecting port visits when possible, improving communications home, ensuring crews get decent food and mail, and finding opportunities for rest. These things may seem small compared with the operational mission, but anyone who’s spent time deployed knows how much they matter. At home, it means making existing family support programs work better. Childcare, emergency assistance and spouse employment support shouldn’t require families to navigate a maze of offices and paperwork. The Navy has programs and resources available. The question is whether they’re easy to access and responsive when people need them. And when ships return, commanders should have the flexibility to ease off requirements that can wait. Not every inspection, training event or administrative task needs to happen immediately after a crew has spent nearly a year at sea. Readiness matters. So does recognizing when people need a break. This may be the toughest part. Operational schedules change. Ships break. Crises happen. Combatant commanders need forces. No one is suggesting the Navy can eliminate those realities. But families need some ability to plan their lives. When deployment schedules, transfers and post-deployment requirements are constantly shifting, even routine decisions become difficult. The Navy should be looking for more flexibility in permanent change of station timing, better coordination between operational and personnel commands, and greater protection for post-deployment recovery periods. That last point deserves particular attention. A Sailor coming home after eleven months at sea doesn’t simply pick up where things left off. Children have grown and changed. Spouses have spent nearly a year handling everything themselves. Families need time to get back into a routine. Giving them that time isn’t a favor. It’s part of keeping Sailors and families healthy enough to continue serving. There’s sometimes a tendency in the military to treat discussions about quality of life as if they’re somehow at odds with warfighting toughness. They aren’t. The Navy needs tough Sailors. It needs people who can endure hardship, operate under pressure and accomplish difficult missions. That’s never going to change. But it also needs leaders who recognize the toll those missions take. A commanding officer who makes communications home a priority isn’t weakening a crew. A senior enlisted leader who helps resolve a family problem isn’t lowering standards. And a fleet commander who protects recovery time after a long deployment isn’t compromising readiness. That’s simply good leadership. There’s also a very practical reason to get this right. The Navy cannot afford to lose experienced Sailors because their families decide that another deployment, another extension or another disrupted year is simply too much. Replacing those Sailors takes time and money. More importantly, the experience they take with them cannot be quickly replaced. The Navy needs more ships, more repair capacity and a stronger maritime industrial base. Admiral Caudle is right to keep pushing those priorities, and Congress and the administration need to help deliver them. But the Sailors deploying today can’t wait for the fleet of the 2030s. There are encouraging signs from Navy leadership. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao has demonstrated a willingness to engage directly with Sailors and put people at the center of his leadership approach. That example matters, particularly when the demands on the force are growing. Combined with the candor shown by Admiral Caudle and MCPON John Perryman, there’s an opportunity to make real progress. The challenge is ensuring that attention at the top translates into meaningful changes throughout the Fleet. Moran’s Trust, Balance and Stability framework provides a useful test. Are we being straight with Sailors and families? Are we doing what we can to ease the burden? Are we giving people enough predictability to manage their lives? These aren’t complicated questions. But answering them honestly, and acting on the answers, takes leadership. The Navy can’t control every operational demand, and it certainly can’t produce new ships overnight. But it has considerable control over how it manages the people it already has. If longer deployments are going to be the norm, then the Navy needs to adjust how it supports the Sailors and families being asked to live with them. We need tough warfighters and resilient families. We also need compassionate leaders who understand that taking care of people is part of maintaining a combat-ready Navy. The Navy can’t build its way out of this problem overnight. But it can lead its way through it, starting now. Chris Servello is co-founder of Provision Advisors and co-host of the CavasShips podcast . articles.title: Venezuelan Oil Exports Remain Stable Despite Stagnant Production, High Freight Rates
articles.summary: Venezuela's oil exports were little changed at 1.08 million barrels per day in October as stagnant crude production and high freight rates continued to curb demand for many South American grades, according to shipping data seen by Reuters on…
articles.body: Venezuelan Oil Exports Remain Stable Despite Stagnant Production, High Freight Rates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © Adobe Stock/hamara Venezuela's oil exports were little changed at 1.08 million barrels per day in October as stagnant crude production and high freight rates continued to curb demand for many South American grades, according to shipping data seen by Reuters on Tuesday. The country's oil output and exports have rebounded this year to near pre-sanctions levels following the US capture of then-President Nicolas Maduro in January and a flagship agreement with global traders overseen by Washington. However, growth has recently plateaued as Venezuela's oil and gas producers prepare investments to expand production capacity through imports of drilling rigs and equipment and repairs to state-run PDVSA's ageing infrastructure. A total of 67 vessels departed Venezuelan waters in October carrying crude, fuel, oil products and petrochemicals. Export volumes were down 0.5% from September and the lowest since February, but were 21% higher than a year earlier, the data showed. Exports to the US, the largest destination for Venezuelan crude, fell nearly 29% from the previous month to about 449,000 bpd. Shipments to Europe rose to 235,000 bpd from 86,000 bpd in September. Exports to India edged down to 242,000 bpd from 253,000 bpd, while shipments to Caribbean storage hubs increased to 83,000 bpd from 76,000 bpd. Chevron's exports of Venezuelan crude rose to about 303,000 bpd, their second highest monthly average this year. Shipments handled by traders including Vitol and Trafigura fell to about 506,000 bpd from 637,000 bpd in September, according to the data, which combines PDVSA exports records and vessel-tracking information. (Reuters)

articles.title: Oil Services Industry Face Cost Pressures Amidst Iran Crisis
articles.summary: The Iran conflict is causing the oil services industry to increase its cost assessment for projects due to rising shipment, fuel and security costs, which are affecting its Middle Eastern contract performance, executives said at a conference in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday.The Iran war…
articles.body: Oil Services Industry Face Cost Pressures Amidst Iran Crisis Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Photocreo Bednarek The Iran conflict is causing the oil services industry to increase its cost assessment for projects due to rising shipment, fuel and security costs, which are affecting its Middle Eastern contract performance, executives said at a conference in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. The Iran war, now in its ninth month, has damaged infrastructure and forced staff to evacuate in several countries. Threats to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz have made equipment deliveries difficult, increasing the cost of both labour and insurance. “What we are facing now with our contracts in the Middle East is that logistics costs have increased - sometimes threefold. Fuel costs have doubled, labour costs have increased 30 to 40 percent,” said Alessandro Bernini, chief executive of Italian engineering group Maire. The cost jump is eating into margins of service companies, raising the cost of projects and ultimately translating into higher energy prices and inflation around the world, he said. Logistics have become a problem due to the difficulty of delivering equipment, said Alessandro Puliti, CEO of Italian energy contractor Saipem. “We have been sitting outside Hormuz for months,” he told the conference. Oil services company NESR, which has operations in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman and Iraq, said the biggest increase in costs was in shipping and logistics, as it had to store materials in warehouses for much longer to cover for possible disruptions. Companies are absorbing those cost increases, its CEO said. “You eat it most of the time. You are not happy but you just move on. C’est la vie,” said NESR chief executive Sherif Foda. (Reuters)

articles.title: Euronaval 2026 Meets Amidst Global Maritime Defense Threats
articles.summary: Shipbuilders, missile makers and drone manufacturers showcased their wares at an arms fair starting near Paris on Tuesday, as European governments, doubting the United States as a defence ally and alarmed by Russian aggression, rush to bolster navies.The increasing use of drones at sea…
articles.body: Euronaval 2026 Meets Amidst Global Maritime Defense Threats Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © Adobe Stock/aerial-drone Shipbuilders, missile makers and drone manufacturers showcased their wares at an arms fair starting near Paris on Tuesday, as European governments, doubting the United States as a defence ally and alarmed by Russian aggression, rush to bolster navies. The increasing use of drones at sea, attacks on critical undersea infrastructure and the targeting of commercial shipping in conflicts including in the Middle East mark a shift in the challenges that European naval forces face. Last month, NATO said it would send more maritime patrol aircraft and drones to the Black Sea in response to a spate of deadly drone attacks on cargo vessels off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts linked to Russia's war in Ukraine. Organisers expect a record number of exhibitors at the November 3-6 Euronaval defence exhibition, rising 45% from the previous edition two years ago. The market for military and paramilitary shipbuilding was worth $122 billion globally in 2024-2025, up 50% from two years prior, the organisers say. DRONES A FOCUS OF ATTENTION Defence groups including France's Naval Group, Germany's TKMS and European missile maker MBDA are showing products ranging from warships to combat software and naval ammunition. Drones were likely to attract particular attention, said Rear Admiral Guillaume Merveilleux du Vignaux, Euronaval's general commissioner. Drones at sea have various military uses, from autonomous underwater systems monitoring undersea cables or looking for mines, to surface ones used for surveillance or destruction on impact, specialists say. One such product, a suicide drone, so named because it destroys itself once used, to help protect ports and vessels, was unveiled by defence group KNDS and French startup SeaOwl. Speaking at the show, French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin pledged to set up an initiative to help large manufacturers and startups collaborate further on developing sea drones. The French government launched a similar "pact" for aerial drones in 2024, which led to collaborations including one between the French carmaker Renault and drone manufacturer Turgis et Gaillard to build a long-range suicide drone. Beyond simply buying drones, officials say the challenge is to connect these new systems to ships or submarines built years or decades ago. Operating drones at sea also presents technical difficulties not encountered on land, from movement at sea to interference created by ships' radar or their steel hulls. "A ship at sea moves a lot," a French Navy official said last week at a press conference. "All of the GPS-based systems need to take that into account." Military officials and industry executives say a parallel challenge is identifying who is behind attacks as unclaimed operations at sea, in particular involving drones, become more common. Industry experts say they are now betting on AI to help with that. "AI will enable important progress" to handle big quantities of data captured by radars and sensors, Merveilleux du Vignaux said. (Reuters)

articles.title: Hormuz Standoff Leaves Both Sides With Economic Pain
articles.summary: As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS By Gerry Doyle (Bloomberg) — As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff. For Iran, the US blockade of its oil exports has snuffed out a key part of its military funding and severely hobbled the $300 billion economy, with only a tiny fraction of the prewar 2 million barrels per day are leaving the country via land routes. And for the US, the rising cost of shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz — even though US Central Command says almost all Iranian attacks there fail or are intercepted — has kept fuel prices high, stirring a political backlash at home with the midterm elections fast approaching. Iran doesn’t even need a high tempo of attacks to keep oil prices elevated; although shipments through the strait are at about 80% of prewar levels, the associated risk has inflated insurance costs. It was more expensive in early October to hire a supertanker in some parts of the world than it was to send a rocket into space. But even significant economic pain isn’t likely to change Iran’s ability to keep up “harassing fire” in the strait, said Jim Lamson, a visiting research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and former CIA analyst focused on Iran and the Middle East. A stockpile of missile components means Tehran can continue to assemble anti-ship weapons, even though US airstrikes have severely degraded its ability to manufacture them at scale, he said. “They have been planning for a long-term asymmetric conflict with the US for decades,” Lamson said. “Things like building in resilience, building in redundancy, building in stockpiling — these have been part of their military culture.” Although there were a record of at least 28 open-source reports of damage to shipping in the strait in October, Iran has not increased its volume of attacks, according to a US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Instead, more serious damage has led to more incidents being flagged, with a quarter of the reports in the first two weeks of October involving strikes on ships’ engine rooms, which can take vessels out of service. US forces reportedly struck Iranian positions on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz overnight. Trump, meanwhile, has expressed hope for negotiations. The continued attacks by Iran leave a few options — none of them with a guaranteed favorable outcome. Trump may order the resumption of airstrikes after the election, even though these only go so far to completely shut down Iran’s ability to lob missiles into the strait — typically unsophisticated weapons that attack any ship in a target area. That leaves making the economic cost of Iranian ship attacks impossible to bear, said John Miller, a retired US Navy vice admiral and former head of the Navy element of CENTCOM. “As long as they want to have a blockade in place, they can continue to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz,” Miller said of Iran. “This has always been the case: You can either make them unwilling or unable.” The tanker industry is continuing to send oil out of the Middle East for now at near prewar levels, and it’s not clear what sort of escalation it would take to halt that. Transits through the waterway are earning owners of supertankers tens of millions of dollars, and the vessels’ crews several months’ pay for a few days of dangerous navigation. For now that’s proving sufficient to keep trade running. The International Maritime Organization estimates that there have been 121 incidents in Hormuz and the wider region since the war began, including 24 confirmed seafarer fatalities. No ship has struck a floating mine while transiting the strait, the US official said, although Iran said as recently as late October that a mine damaged a tanker, and on Friday the UKMTO, which monitors shipping security, reported a tanker was damaged by explosives placed on its hull. Iran is using both traditional cruise missiles and drones to attack shipping, the official said, and US forces are both organizing ship transits and protecting them, largely with aircraft overhead. CENTCOM has said about 95% of ships transit the strait without incident. The US works directly with the shipping industry, sharing information and discussing timing, routes and numbers for vessels that want to pass through the strait in either direction, the US official said. US forces then formulate a plan for doing so safely, including what assets will be used to keep tabs on the journey and shoot down threats if necessary. Miller said much of Iran’s ability to track anything beyond visual range of its shores had been all but destroyed over the last eight months. As a result, the weapons it uses are often fired blind, or at the general area where Iranian strike planners think ships might be. Once the missiles arrive, radar or infrared seekers guide them to whatever is nearby. Aircraft armed with cheap munitions such as the APKWS missile, which costs about $20,000 for a BAE Systems Plc guidance kit, handle those sorts of attacks. The expensive and advanced air-defense interceptors on US Navy ships, such as the Raytheon SM-6 and SM-3 Block IIA, are then reserved for ballistic missile threats. Trump has previewed in recent days plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. But it’s not clear that airstrikes — especially against an adversary that has planned for decades to keep key capabilities safe against such attacks — will change the situation in the strait, said Emma Salisbury, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an associate fellow at the Royal Navy Strategic Studies Centre. A surge in fighting could push oil prices into the $120-$130 range, according to analysis by Bloomberg Economics chief emerging markets economist Ziad Daoud. Both sides “may prefer a brief conflict to improve their negotiating power,” he wrote. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Qatar’s US LNG Bet Signals a New Energy Order
articles.summary: Turning to your biggest rival is rarely a sign of confidence. Yet Qatar's decision to sign long-term contracts for US supplies suggests the world's second-largest LNG exporter is increasingly concerned that instability in the Gulf could undermine its ambitious expansion plans.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Image: Shutterstock/Oleksandr Kalinichenko By Ron Bousso LONDON, Nov 3 (Reuters) – Turning to your biggest rival is rarely a sign of confidence. Yet Qatar’s decision to sign long-term contracts for US supplies suggests the world’s second-largest LNG exporter is increasingly concerned that instability in the Gulf could undermine its ambitious expansion plans. QatarEnergy last week signed a 20-year agreement to buy 3 million metric tons per year (mtpa) of liquefied natural gas from Woodside Energy’s facilities in Louisiana. A week earlier, it signed agreements with Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi plants through 2054. Deliveries under the contracts begin in 2030 and 2031 and will make Qatar the largest buyer of US LNG. QatarEnergy CEO Saad al-Kaabi told Reuters last week that he expects to sign additional supply agreements with US and other producers this year, potentially locking in millions of tons of overseas LNG for decades to come. Before the US-Iran war broke out on February 28, the state-owned company had already been expanding internationally. It had been acquiring stakes in LNG projects from North America to Africa as part of a strategy to broaden its trading portfolio and gain greater flexibility. The latest deals, however, reflect a more fundamental shift. Rather than simply diversifying its portfolio, Qatar now appears to be buying insurance against disruptions to its own exports. Qatar’s purchases are another sign that the US has not so quietly emerged as the biggest beneficiary of the global rethink of Middle East energy risk, marking a historical reversal of roles. “Twenty-five years ago my White House colleagues and I worried the US would become as dependent on Qatar for LNG as we were on OPEC for oil,” said Bob McNally, founder and president of Rapidan Energy Group and a former White House energy advisor to President George W. Bush. “Then came the shale revolution and Iran War, and now Qatar is buying from us,” McNally said. INSURANCE POLICY As Washington and Tehran continue to spar over the future of the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf producers are racing to reduce their reliance on the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of global energy supplies flowed before the war. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are expanding, or preparing to expand, pipeline networks that bypass Hormuz to improve their ability to export crude oil and refined fuels outside the Gulf. Qatar faces a far more difficult challenge. Unlike its neighbors, the small Gulf state has no viable route for exporting LNG other than Hormuz. Its entire LNG industry is concentrated at its giant Ras Laffan facility, where gas from the North Field is processed and shipped to customers around the world. The conflict made those risks painfully clear in March, when an Iranian missile damaged two of QatarEnergy’s 14 LNG trains at Ras Laffan, removing about 17% of the country’s export capability. QatarEnergy said the outage would cost roughly $20 billion a year in lost revenue and that repairs would take around three years. Any effort by Qatar to develop alternative export infrastructure would require tens of billions of dollars of investment in pipelines and liquefaction capacity. Even then, building massive new energy facilities simply creates more sites vulnerable to attack, as the war has demonstrated. It is therefore unsurprising that Qatar’s strategy is to seek protection not by building more domestic infrastructure but through geographic diversification. A TWO-HORSE RACE The current challenges come at a particularly difficult time for Qatar, as the Gulf state embarks on its biggest growth push in decades. The International Energy Agency estimates that roughly 300 billion cubic meters of new LNG export capacity will come online worldwide between 2025 and 2030, increasing available global supply by around 50%. More than half of that new capacity will come from the US, while Qatar is expected to account for roughly another quarter. The two countries are therefore set to dominate growth in global LNG trade over the coming decade, setting up an increasingly intense competition for market share. Qatari LNG still has some distinct benefits over US supplies, most notably production costs. Industry estimates place Qatari costs at roughly $3-$5 per million British thermal units, about half the cost of many US projects. Washington, however, enjoys one critical advantage: American LNG exporters face none of the geopolitical constraints associated with dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. This was not previously a major concern, but in the wake of the Iran war, oil and gas buyers increasingly value security of supply as highly as price. The question is no longer whether QatarEnergy’s plans to nearly double LNG production by 2030 will remain on track. The first new trains are expected to start operations early next year. The question is whether those facilities will actually remain operational in a radically reshaped Gulf. Even if the US and Iran eventually agree to a sustainable peace deal in the coming months – a big “if” – the role of Hormuz in regional energy markets has likely changed forever, to Qatar’s disadvantage. The days of guaranteed access through the waterway appear to be over. For Qatar, then, purchasing US LNG offers a way to profit from growing demand for politically secure supplies, even if those supplies come from North America. This may be the strongest evidence yet that the Iran conflict has accelerated the decade-long shift in energy market power away from the Middle East and toward the US. articles.summary: New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill is warning port and terminal operators not to accept Russian diesel shipments heading toward the U.S. East Coast, arguing that the Trump administration’s authorization of...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Igor Karasi / Shutterstock New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill is warning port and terminal operators not to accept Russian diesel shipments heading toward the U.S. East Coast, arguing that the Trump administration’s authorization of the imports violates federal law and could leave businesses facing millions of dollars in penalties. In a letter sent Monday , Sherrill urged operators to turn away tankers carrying Russian fuel and pledged to use New Jersey’s legal and regulatory powers to prevent the shipments from being unloaded at the state’s terminals. The warning comes as at least one tanker carrying Russian diesel continues toward the U.S. East Coast following the Trump administration’s decision last month to temporarily allow Russian diesel imports in an effort to ease soaring fuel prices. “Every port and terminal operator, intermediary, and buyer is on notice: do not help bring illegal Russian diesel into New Jersey,” Sherrill said. The dispute centers on General License 135 , issued October 9 by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The license authorizes transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. Sherrill argues that the license conflicts with the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, passed by Congress in April 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The law banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products, including diesel. According to the governor, the law does not give the president or Treasury Department broad authority to lift the ban without congressional approval. She also argues that the authorization should have undergone a congressional review process before taking effect. In her letter, Sherrill warned that companies participating in an unlawful importation could face penalties equal to the value of the cargo under federal customs law, potentially amounting to millions of dollars. The Treasury Department has maintained that its authorization complies with applicable law, leaving port operators caught between the federal government’s decision to permit the shipments and warnings from state officials and lawmakers that handling the cargo could expose them to future legal action. The warning comes as the Malta-flagged product tanker Agioi Fanendes continues its voyage after loading approximately 40,000 metric tons of diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. The vessel initially listed New York as its destination, with an expected arrival around November 7, but later changed its AIS destination to “for orders,” leaving its intended discharge port uncertain. According to a November 3 assessment by maritime intelligence firm Windward , Agioi Fanendes appears to be the only one of three Russian diesel tankers previously reported as heading toward the United States that remains on a course toward the U.S. East Coast. Two other tankers, Talisman and Leruo , have changed their declared destinations, suggesting their plans may have changed. Windward said no Russian diesel cargo has yet been delivered to the United States under the new authorization. Sherrill’s warning follows a similar move by Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), who last week called on the owner of Agioi Fanendes to turn the tanker around , arguing that the federal license cannot override the 2022 import ban. The growing opposition adds another complication for shipowners, charterers and terminal operators considering whether to participate in the trade. Sherrill also criticized the administration for allowing purchases of Russian fuel while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine and provides support to Iran, where U.S. forces remain engaged in hostilities. The governor, a former Navy helicopter pilot, said New Jersey would not allow its ports to help finance those activities. For now, it remains unclear whether any Russian diesel tanker will attempt to discharge at a New Jersey terminal. But with Agioi Fanendes still at sea and its destination unconfirmed, the legal and political pressure surrounding the shipment continues to grow. articles.body: Ryder System has acquired Efficiency Enterprises, expanding its truck rental, leasing and maintenance network across the eastern United States. The acquisition closed on 1 November 2026. As a result, Ryder adds six facilities across Florida, New York, Maryland and Delaware. The deal also brings approximately 1,200 fleet and equipment units into Ryder’s operations. These include more than 900 truck and trailer units and over 200 material handling equipment units. In addition, around 50 technicians will join the company’s Fleet Management Solutions (FMS) business. Ryder expands across six US markets The acquisition adds facilities in Orlando, Tampa and Fort Myers in Florida, Astoria in New York, Baltimore in Maryland, and Middletown in Delaware. These locations serve important transportation and distribution markets. For example, Baltimore provides access to port-related freight activity, while Astoria supports urban deliveries across New York City. Meanwhile, Central Florida continues to attract logistics operations linked to distribution, e-commerce and food transportation. According to Ryder, the expanded network will help customers access fleet maintenance, truck leasing and rental services across more locations. Tom Havens, President of Fleet Management Solutions at Ryder, said the acquisition strengthens the company’s ability to support customers in high-demand logistics markets. Efficiency Enterprises was founded in Astoria in 1978. Since then, it has expanded its operations across several eastern states, providing fleet management, maintenance and equipment leasing services. Acquisition expected to support revenue growth Ryder expects Efficiency Enterprises to generate approximately US$50 million in gross revenue for its FMS business in 2027. The company also expects the acquisition to contribute to earnings. However, it has not disclosed the purchase price. Meanwhile, Ryder plans to integrate the acquired operations into its existing network during the remainder of 2026. Richard Barbato Jr., President of Efficiency Enterprises, will support the transition to help maintain uninterrupted services for customers. Overall, the acquisition supports Ryder’s strategy to expand its fleet services network across major US freight corridors. It also increases the company’s capacity to serve transportation and distribution businesses.

Join the leading maritime news network default Damen Shipyards Group and Windcat are pleased to announce that Commissioning Service Operations Vessel (CSOV) Windcat Rotterdam has received the KNVTS Ship of the Year Award. The award was presented at the Maritime Awards Gala on 2 November in Hilversum, the Netherlands. Integrated innovation Every year, the KNVTS (Koninklijke Nederlandse Vereniging van Technici op Scheepsbouwgebied; Royal Society of Dutch Marine Engineers) presents the Ship of the Year Award to a highly innovative vessel designed in the Netherlands. The award is presented to a Dutch shipyard that integrates innovations into the vessel, ensures effective collaboration between parties involved, and delivers a high-performing ship to the client. Nominations are judged by a panel of maritime experts, who assess the vessel on a range of criteria comprising design, economics, sustainability & environment, safety and the construction process. Collaborative development Windcat Rotterdam has been developed through a collaboration between Damen, Windcat and CMB.TECH. It is the first of six Elevation Series vessels. The CSOV is designed to support construction, commissioning and maintenance at offshore energy projects. The vessel serves as a floating base for both personnel and equipment, facilitating safe, efficient access to offshore assets. It features a standard-setting 3D motion-compensated gangway with a high vertical range. Additionally, it boasts the world’s first 10-ton 3D motion-compensated crane, enabling the safe execution of heavier platform lifts in high sea states. Home-away-from-home experience The interior of the CSOV has been developed in collaboration with experts to provide personnel with a home-away-from-home experience. It offers comfortable accommodation for up to 120 people in spacious single and double cabins. It also has a fully equipped gym and entertainment spaces to provide a range of leisure activities. Personnel onboard also benefit from high-quality catering facilities and housekeeping services. Future-ready Windcat Rotterdam , like the Elevation Series in general, has been designed for optimal efficiency. It is equipped with the latest in fuel-efficient and emissions control technology, including a closed bus switchboard configuration and hybrid battery-electric propulsion. Safe and sustainable offshore operations rely on an effective and efficient dynamic positioning system. Damen’s DPX-DRIVE™ technology delivers best-in-class DP performance. With this, four azimuth thrusters enable precision maneuverability and efficient operation, enhancing safety while reducing fuel consumption and associated emissions. Additionally, the CSOV draws on the experience Windcat has gained with its hydrogen-powered crew transfer vessels (CTVs) to ensure future readiness. CMB.TECH’s hydrogen technology is integrated into the vessel. Once final class approval for the solution is secured, the vessel will be outfitted with a hydrogen generator set, storage and fuel supply. Damen Director Benelux, Joost van der Weiden says, “ Windcat Rotterdam serves as a clear demonstration of the power of collaboration. Together with Windcat and CMB.TECH, we have developed a vessel with the capabilities to provide efficient support to the offshore energy industry , not only for today, but also for the years to come. On behalf of everyone at Damen, I accept the prestigious Ship of the Year Award with pride.” Willem van der Wel, Managing Director at Windcat, said, “I congratulate Damen on receiving the Ship of the Year Award for the Windcat Rotterdam . This award is a well-deserved recognition of what can be achieved through close collaboration, combining Damen’s shipbuilding expertise with Windcat’soperational experience and shared ambition to innovate. Together, we have developed a CSOV that brings advanced technology and practical capabilities together to support the offshore energy sector safely and efficiently.” Chair of the Jury Koos Ziman said, “ The Windcat Rotterdam is a deserving winner, because it is a complex vessel that required close collaboration between different disciplines. The logistics have been well thought out, making it highly practical for the crew. And a homely atmosphere has also been created for the crew, so they can feel comfortable during their long periods at sea.” The award marks an important milestone for both Damen and Windcat, recognising their shared commitment to the development of increasingly sustainable offshore solutions. articles.summary: The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) has banned a Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier from Australian ports for 90 days after inspectors discovered that crew work and rest records had been...

Photo courtesy AMSA The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) has banned a Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier from Australian ports for 90 days after inspectors discovered that crew work and rest records had been deliberately falsified to conceal excessive working hours. The ban against the Wooyang Venus follows an October 29 port State control inspection in Newcastle prompted by a complaint under the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC). Inspectors found that the vessel’s records did not accurately reflect the hours worked by its crew. It marks the third detention of the vessel in Australian waters in less than three years, with previous inspections uncovering similar problems. According to AMSA , the Wooyang Venus was detained in August 2026 after inspectors found that crew work and rest hours were not being properly recorded or monitored. The vessel was also detained in December 2023 over incorrect work and rest records. That earlier detention involved more serious crew welfare concerns. According to AMSA’s 2023 Maritime Labour Convention annual report , inspectors responding to a complaint from the International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) found poor-quality food provisions, falsified working-hour records and evidence that the ship’s master had physically assaulted a seafarer. The operator subsequently submitted a corrective action plan that included crew repatriation arrangements, improved food provisions and additional training on work and rest hour compliance. Despite those measures, similar deficiencies have continued to surface. Greg Witherall, AMSA’s Executive Director of Maritime Safety and Environmental Compliance, warned that falsifying records intended to protect seafarers poses serious risks to both crews and maritime safety. “Evidence has shown poor fatigue management can impair judgement, reduce alertness and slow reaction times,” Witherall said. He warned that fatigue increases the risk of collisions, groundings and serious injuries, particularly during navigation, watchkeeping and other safety-critical operations. Under the MLC, shipowners and operators must comply with minimum standards covering seafarers’ working and living conditions, including mandatory rest periods. Accurate recordkeeping is essential to demonstrating compliance and preventing fatigue-related incidents. AMSA said the 90-day ban was imposed under Section 246 of Australia’s Navigation Act 2012, citing the deliberate falsification of records, repeated deficiencies and concerns about the effectiveness of the vessel owner’s and operator’s safety management systems. The agency has identified crewing and fatigue management as a key enforcement priority under its 2026–27 National Compliance Plan. “Where we find serious or repeated failures to meet those obligations, AMSA will take strong action,” Witherall said. November 3, 2026 © RTsys Group At Euronaval 2026, RTsys Group announced the sale of several SEMA training targets to two Canadian defense agencies: Defense Research and Development Canada (DRDC) and the Naval Engineering Test Establishment (NETE). This marks a new international milestone for its anti-submarine warfare (ASW) solution. Developed by RTsys Underwater Technologies, a subsidiary of the group, SEMA is a recoverable acoustic target designed to train naval forces in anti-submarine warfare (ASW). It simulates the presence of a submarine, trains operators in its detection and tracking, and enables torpedo-firing exercises without deploying an actual submarine. The solution is notably compatible with modern sonars and the latest-generation torpedoes. Unveiled at Euronaval 2026, the third-generation target, SEMA MK-Ill, marks a new technological milestone. In particular, it incorporates the ability to simulate a submarine's magnetic signature, in addition to its acoustic signature. Equipped with an Iridium satellite link and now recoverable by helicopter winch, it expands training capabilities, particularly for missions conducted from helicopters. New software also facilitates mission planning and monitoring. As a supplier to several NATO navies in North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region, RTsys Group is continuing to expand its presence in the submarine defense market. The group will be exhibiting at Euronaval 2026, November 3-6 at Paris Nord Villepinte (Hall 6, Booth F99), where it will also showcase two other new products: SONADIVE MK-II and SONABLOW.

articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd and Ocean Network Express (ONE) are warning customers that most of the cargo aboard the fire-damaged containership Espirito Santo Express is likely severely damaged or a total loss, more...

Join the leading maritime news network File Photo: Hapag-Lloyd Hapag-Lloyd and Ocean Network Express (ONE) are warning customers that most of the cargo aboard the fire-damaged containership Espirito Santo Express is likely severely damaged or a total loss, more than two weeks after a fire broke out aboard the vessel in the South Atlantic. In separate customer advisories, both shipping companies said they had received information from vessel owner Seaspan indicating that the vast majority of cargo may be beyond recovery. “Based on the latest information received via the vessel owner Seaspan we expect the vast majority of the cargo to be either severely damaged by the fire or a total loss,” Hapag-Lloyd said in its latest update. The fire is now under control, but the vessel has yet to reach a port of refuge, where the full extent of the damage can be assessed. Hapag-Lloyd warned that getting the ship to safety and inspecting the cargo will take considerable time. ONE issued a similar warning, confirming the assessment from Seaspan. The vessel was operating on ONE’s East Coast South America Express 1 (SX1) service. For customers with cargo aboard, the outlook is grim, although the condition of individual containers remains unknown. Hapag-Lloyd said it will contact customers whose shipments may be salvageable to arrange cargo surveys once the vessel reaches port and an initial damage assessment is completed. The 11,800-TEU Espirito Santo Express , a Singapore-flagged containership built in 2018 and chartered by Hapag-Lloyd from Seaspan, caught fire on October 15 while sailing from Singapore to Santos, Brazil. According to an October 22 statement from Seaspan, smoke and then flames were observed coming from cargo in a bay forward of the vessel’s accommodation block. All 28 crew members abandoned ship and were rescued by the Portuguese-flagged bulk carrier Aeolian Arrow. The rescue, however, was marked by tragedy when the bulk carrier’s chief officer fell overboard while its rescue boat was being recovered. He disappeared beneath the water and could not be recovered, according to Portuguese maritime accident investigators. Firefighting and salvage operations continued in the days that followed. As recently as October 22, Hapag-Lloyd said the extent of the damage remained unknown and it could not determine the condition of individual shipments. The latest warnings from Hapag-Lloyd and ONE provide the clearest indication yet of the scale of the losses, although a full assessment will have to wait until the ship reaches a port of refuge. The cause of the fire remains under investigation, and neither carrier has provided a timeline for when the vessel might reach port. articles.summary: The former USS Enterprise (CVN 65), the world’s first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, departed Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia under tow on Monday, November 2, beginning its final journey to Mobile,...

Join the leading maritime news network The former USS Enterprise (CVN 65) departs Newport News Shipbuilding under tow on November 2, 2026, bound for dismantling in Mobile, Alabama. Photo: HII. The former USS Enterprise (CVN 65), the world’s first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, departed Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia under tow on Monday, November 2, beginning its final journey to Mobile, Alabama, where the historic warship will be dismantled. The departure marks another milestone in the retirement of one of the U.S. Navy’s most storied vessels, nearly 14 years after the carrier completed its final deployment and almost a decade after its formal decommissioning. Known as the “Big E,” Enterprise spent more than five decades in service, becoming a symbol of American naval power and pioneering the use of nuclear propulsion aboard aircraft carriers. The ship is headed to a commercial dismantling facility in Mobile, where NorthStar Maritime Dismantlement Services will carry out the work under a $418.5 million Navy contract awarded in July 2026. The project includes dismantling, recycling and disposal of the entire vessel, including its eight defueled nuclear reactor plants. The work is expected to be completed by September 2030. The move follows the Navy’s 2023 decision to pursue commercial dismantling rather than relying on public shipyards. The Navy determined that the commercial approach could reduce disposal costs by approximately half compared with other alternatives, shorten the dismantling timeline and free up public shipyard capacity for fleet maintenance. The project will also serve as a test case for the eventual disposal of the Navy’s Nimitz-class nuclear-powered aircraft carriers. NorthStar has partnered with Modern American Recycling and Radiological Services, part of Modern American Recycling Services, to perform the dismantling work in Mobile. Materials recovered from the ship will be recycled where possible, while low-level radioactive waste and other hazardous materials will be transported to authorized disposal facilities. Commissioned on November 25, 1961, Enterprise was the first aircraft carrier powered by nuclear reactors and the eighth U.S. Navy vessel to carry the name. At 1,123 feet long overall, the ship was among the largest warships ever built and was powered by eight nuclear reactors driving four propeller shafts. Throughout its career, Enterprise participated in some of the most significant U.S. military operations of the past half-century, including the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Vietnam War and combat operations in Afghanistan and Iraq. In 1964, Enterprise participated in Operation Sea Orbit, joining the nuclear-powered cruiser USS Long Beach and destroyer leader USS Bainbridge in a historic around-the-world voyage without refueling. By the time it completed its final deployment in 2012, Enterprise had traveled more than one million nautical miles under nuclear power. The carrier was formally inactivated in December 2012 and decommissioned on February 3, 2017 , becoming the first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in U.S. Navy history to undergo the process. Its nuclear fuel was removed at Newport News Shipbuilding, where the vessel remained while the Navy developed its disposal plan. “Enterprise will always be remembered for her proud legacy of service, a legacy made possible by the Sailors and support personnel whose dedication kept her mission-ready,” said Kevin Cormier, Deputy Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maritime for Aircraft Carriers, in a statement announcing the departure . “All who served aboard and sustained this historic ship should take pride in the vital role they played in supporting the fleet.” While the original nuclear-powered Enterprise is headed for dismantling, its name will live on aboard the future USS Enterprise (CVN 80), a Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier currently under construction at Newport News Shipbuilding. articles.body: Hanwha Defense USA has secured its first US Navy shipbuilding contract after being selected by TOTE Services to construct a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) at Hanwha Philly Shipyard. The initial contract is valued at US$269 million and covers one vessel, with options for three additional ships. The agreement marks an important step in Hanwha’s expansion into US naval shipbuilding. The selection was announced by TOTE Services on 30 October 2026 and confirmed by Hanwha on 2 November. Construction scheduled to begin in 2027 Construction of the first LSM is expected to begin during the fourth quarter of 2027 at Hanwha’s Philadelphia facility. The project forms part of the US Navy and Marine Corps’ broader LSM programme, which envisages a fleet of 35 vessels. TOTE Services manages vessel construction under a US$2.2 billion Vessel Construction Manager (VCM) contract. However, this figure relates to the wider programme and not the individual Hanwha award. The first vessel under the LSM programme is expected to be delivered in 2030. According to Hanwha, preparations for naval construction have been underway at the Philadelphia shipyard since earlier this year. Michael Coulter, President and CEO of Hanwha Defense USA, said the company has invested in workforce development and technology since acquiring Philly Shipyard in 2024. Meanwhile, TOTE Services President Jeff Dixon said the construction management approach had helped accelerate the contracting process. Rendering of an LSM, which HDUSA will construct at Hanwha Philly Shipyard Hanwha expands Philadelphia shipbuilding operations The contract adds naval shipbuilding to Hanwha Philly Shipyard’s existing commercial vessel construction activities. The shipyard has previously built and delivered four National Security Multi-Mission Vessels under the VCM model in cooperation with TOTE Services. It is also involved in commercial shipbuilding projects, including containership construction for Matson. Hanwha Defense USA plans to draw on this experience as it prepares to build the new landing ship. The company also announced that it is pursuing a controlling stake in Hanwha Philly Shipyard as part of its wider US expansion strategy. The LSM contract represents a further step in Hanwha’s efforts to develop its American shipbuilding operations across both commercial and defence markets.

articles.summary: Norway has detained a Chinese-owned heavy-lift vessel sanctioned for its role in delivering equipment to Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project, in what appears to be the first known detention in the Arctic of a Chinese vessel linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Ya Qing Hai Yang off Vesterålen Islands. (Courtesy of Arctic North Adventures) Norway has detained a Chinese-owned heavy-lift vessel sanctioned for its role in delivering equipment to Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project, in what appears to be the first known detention in the Arctic of a Chinese vessel linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. The Ya Qing Hai Yang was detained after Norwegian inspectors found that it lacked valid flag-state registration and required certificates, the Norwegian Maritime Authority said. The case is a notable enforcement action against a vessel with documented ties to Russia’s sanctioned energy sector, although authorities say the detention was based on maritime safety and registration deficiencies rather than the ship’s sanctions status. The Norwegian Maritime Authority inspected the vessel on October 13 after it sought shelter from bad weather in Andfjorden, off the Vesterålen Islands in northern Norway. “During the inspection, it was discovered that the vessel did not have a valid flag registration and lacked the required certificates,” Dag Inge Aarhus, the authority’s communications director said last week. “The vessel has therefore been detained until further notice.” The vessel remains off the Vesterålen Islands as of November 3. The ship must establish valid registration with a flag state and obtain the necessary certificates before Norwegian authorities can complete the inspection and consider its release. The detention appears to be the first publicly documented case of Norway holding a vessel sailing under an invalid flag registration. It also appears to be the country’s first detention of a vessel associated with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet. The vessel has a history of involvement in Russian energy shipments. In October 2024, when it sailed under the name Ocean 28 , it transported large power-generation modules from China to the Utrenniy terminal , which serves Novatek’s Arctic LNG 2 project on Russia’s Gydan Peninsula. The delivery involved equipment manufactured by China’s Wison New Energies and a complex shipping operation designed to move the modules to Russia despite Western sanctions. The United States sanctioned the vessel’s operator and related entities in January 2025 . The ship was subsequently included on the European Union’s sanctions lists. The detention comes as European governments face growing pressure to enforce maritime restrictions against vessels involved in Russia’s efforts to sustain its energy exports. Norway had previously emphasized monitoring and voluntary checks of insurance documentation rather than boarding or detaining suspected shadow-fleet vessels. The latest case, however, does not necessarily signal a change in policy: Norwegian authorities say the inspection followed standard procedures after the vessel sought refuge. A second Chinese-owned heavy-lift ship, the Jian Yang Cheng He , was also inspected in Andfjorden but was not detained. Inspectors identified five deficiencies, including poor housekeeping, inadequately protected hot surfaces and documentation requiring updates. The vessel briefly departed the fjord on October 30 after nearly three weeks at anchor, but turned around roughly 12 hours later and returned to shelter. Norway’s Joint Headquarters confirmed that the ship had been allowed to seek shelter again. A yellow warning for strong gales along the coast may have contributed to the decision to turn back. Both vessels traveled from China through the Northern Sea Route during the summer and later appeared near Murmansk and the Norwegian-Russian maritime border. articles.title: DP crews are the new bottleneck: how OSV operators can staff vessels faster
articles.summary: I spent my early career as a deck officer in the merchant fleet, and one lesson from those years has stayed with me through almost two decades of...
articles.body: Branded Content November 3, 2026 · 1 minute ago DP crews are the new bottleneck: how OSV operators can staff vessels faster Written in partnership with Marine MAN 11 minutes read LinkedIn X Email By Pavel Manchenko, Founder and Managing Director, Marine MAN @Marine MAN / jobmarineman.com I spent my early career as a deck officer in the merchant fleet, and one lesson from those years has stayed with me through almost two decades of running a crewing company: a ship is only as good as the people on board. For offshore support vessel operators today, the scarcest resource is often not the vessel but the people who run it. Charter rates, fleet utilisation and newbuilding plans dominate the headlines, yet ask any marine superintendent what keeps them awake and the answer is usually closer to home: who will relieve the Chief Officer on the PSV next month, and does he have enough DP hours to keep his certificate valid? A platform supply vessel, an anchor handler or a construction support vessel on charter earns nothing while it waits for a qualified relief. Every crew change that slips puts pressure on the next one, stretches contracts beyond what seafarers agreed to, and eventually shows up in client audits and incident reports. In a market where skilled offshore crews are in demand across oil and gas, offshore wind and subsea construction, the operators that win are those who treat crewing as a core operational process rather than an administrative afterthought. In this article I look at why offshore crews are so hard to replace, what a late crew change really costs, and six practices that, in our experience at Marine MAN, help operators staff their vessels faster and keep them staffed. Why offshore crews are harder to replace On paper, an officer is an officer. An STCW certificate of competency is the same document whether it was earned on a bulk carrier or an anchor-handling tug. In practice, offshore operations demand a layer of skills that deep-sea trades rarely provide. Dynamic positioning is the most obvious example. A DP operator needs not only formal training but also a documented amount of sea time on DP vessels to obtain the certificate and then keep it. An officer who spends a year on conventional tonnage can find that his DP qualification has quietly lapsed. That makes the pool of officers who are both certified and current much smaller than the headline number of DP certificates suggests. Anchor handling is another. Working on deck during anchor handling and towing operations is high-risk work, and the confidence to do it safely comes from experience under a competent master and bosun, not from a classroom. The same applies to cargo operations alongside installations, where everyone on board must understand exclusion zones, weather limits and communication protocols with the platform. Then there are the clients. Oil majors, national oil companies and offshore contractors audit crew competence before a vessel goes on hire and periodically during the charter. They look at matrices of certificates, sea time on similar vessel types and DP class, and often require a minimum number of years of offshore experience for senior positions. A candidate with an excellent deep-sea record may simply not pass the client's vetting. The result is that a good officer from the merchant fleet is rarely a like-for-like replacement on an OSV. When a DP-critical position falls vacant at short notice, the real choice is often between a handful of suitable candidates, many of whom are already on board other vessels. What a late crew change really costs The direct cost is easy to see. A vessel that cannot sail because a key officer is missing goes off hire or risks penalties under the charter party. Even a single lost day can cost more than a year of crewing fees for that position. The indirect costs are less visible but just as real. When a relief is late, the officer on board is asked to extend. One extension becomes two, fatigue builds up, and the risk of a mistake grows exactly when the vessel is engaged in demanding operations. The Maritime Labour Convention limits how long a seafarer can serve on board before repatriation, so extensions are not an open-ended solution. Seafarers who are repeatedly extended also tend not to come back, which shrinks the pool even further. Late changes are expensive in logistics too. Last-minute flights, hotel stays, launch boats and helicopter seats cost far more than a change planned weeks ahead. And every rushed decision raises the chance of sending someone who does not fully meet the client's requirements, which can trigger a fresh round of audits and, in the worst case, a request to replace the person who has just joined. Practice 1: Plan rotations as a pipeline, not a vacancy The most effective operators stop thinking about vacancies and start thinking about pipelines. For every DP-critical position on every vessel, they know who is on board now, who relieves him next, and who is the backup if the relief falls through. That means keeping the relief identified at least one contract ahead, with certificate expiry dates, DP hours, medicals, visas and client-specific training on file. It means tracking when each officer's DP certificate needs revalidation and making sure his next assignment keeps the sea time flowing. And it means agreeing rotation patterns with seafarers early, so that they plan their lives around the schedule instead of taking another job when the call finally comes. Practice 2: Build a verified talent pool, not a shortlist Traditional recruitment often runs through a chain: the operator asks a manning agent, who asks a sub-agent, who calls his contacts. By the time a shortlist arrives, days have passed and nobody has a clear view of the wider market. Each link in the chain adds cost and removes transparency. That model is changing, and we see it every day on our own platform. More DP officers, engineers and ratings now look for a job at sea directly online, posting their CVs, certificates and sea-service records where shipowners can see them. For operators, this opens access to candidates who are not tied to a single agency and who can be contacted the same day. Direct access only works if the information is reliable. Operators should verify certificates against the issuing administrations, check references from previous masters and companies, and confirm DP logbooks before an offer is made. Over time, the candidates who pass these checks form a verified pool that can be called upon whenever a position opens, instead of starting from zero each time. JobMarineMan: shipowners search a database of 200,000 seafarer profiles and post vacancies directly Marine MAN / jobmarineman.com Practice 3: Measure crew management like any other operational function Fuel consumption, downtime and maintenance backlogs are measured on every well-run vessel. Crewing deserves the same discipline. Treating crew management as an operational function means agreeing on a small set of indicators and reviewing them as seriously as technical performance. Useful indicators include time to fill a vacancy by rank, the share of crew changes made on schedule, the number of contract extensions, retention rate by rank and vessel, and the proportion of candidates who pass client vetting at the first attempt. None of these are complicated to track, yet many companies only discover a crewing problem when a vessel is already short-handed. If crew management is outsourced, the same indicators belong in the service agreement. A provider who reports against them every month gives the operator early warning and a basis for improvement. A provider who only sends invoices does not. Practice 4: Keep the people you already have The fastest way to fill a position is never to lose the person in it. Offshore seafarers have options, and they choose employers who respect their time. Reliable rotations matter more than almost anything else. A seafarer who knows exactly when he will go home, and whose relief turns up on the agreed date, has little reason to look elsewhere. Wages paid on time and in full, clear contract terms and decent conditions on board come next. Career progression is the third factor. Junior DPOs want a path to senior DPO and then to master; engineers want exposure to modern power and propulsion systems. Operators that plan promotions and training, rather than leaving them to chance, keep their best people and build the next generation of DP-qualified officers from within. Every officer promoted internally is one less vacancy to fill from an overheated market. Practice 5: Grow your own DP officers The BIMCO/ICS Seafarer Workforce Report has been warning for years about a shortage of officers, and the offshore sector is named among those where management-level deck officers are hardest to find. Every conference discusses it. Very few companies do anything structural about it. We decided not to wait. JobMarineMan is the first and, as far as I know, still the only crewing platform in the world with a working mentorship programme for seafarers. It is not a plan or a pilot; it is live today. Experienced masters, chief engineers and DP officers apply to become mentors, Marine MAN verifies their sea service and approves them, and from that moment they are visible to every seafarer on the platform. A junior officer picks the mentor whose career looks like the one he wants and contacts him directly; the mentor sets his own terms and agrees them with the seafarer, and we stay out of that conversation. Our job is to make sure every mentor is real, qualified and worth listening to. For an offshore operator, this is a pipeline of the next generation of DP-qualified officers being built today, not a hope that the market will somehow produce them. Mentorship on JobMarineMan: experienced officers and engineers guide the next generation of specialist seafarers Marine MAN / jobmarineman.com Practice 6: Make the first week count Even the best candidate needs time to become effective on a new vessel. Offshore units differ widely in DP systems, deck equipment and company procedures, and the first days on board decide how quickly a new officer settles in. A structured familiarisation programme, a proper handover from the outgoing officer and a clear contact person ashore reduce the risk of errors and make it more likely that the newcomer will return for the next contract. What to ask a crew management partner Many operators outsource part or all of their crewing. The right partner saves time and money; the wrong one simply moves the problem from the operator's desk to a supplier's inbox. A few questions help to tell the difference: • How many DP-qualified officers and offshore-experienced ratings can you present for our vessel types, and how quickly? • How do you verify certificates, DP logbooks and references, and can we see the evidence? • Which countries do you source from, and how do you handle visas and travel for each of them? • How do you handle wages, social obligations and compliance with the Maritime Labour Convention? • Which indicators will you report, and how often? • What happens when a candidate fails client vetting or leaves the vessel early? These are the questions I would ask if I were on the operator's side of the table. Clear answers to them say more about a provider than any brochure. How we work at Marine MAN Marine MAN has worked with shipowners and managers on these questions since 2007. We are an IMO DOC holder and have been certified to ISO 9001:2015 by Bureau Veritas for crew manning and management services since 2017. At any given time, around 750 seafarers serve on board client vessels through Marine MAN, and we source crews from Ukraine, Georgia, India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines. Our platform JobMarineMan, a seaman jobsite available in 11 languages, holds 200,000 seafarer CVs. It connects shipowners and operators with candidates directly, without a chain of intermediaries, while our team takes over verification, documentation and mobilisation when needed. In my experience, offshore operators rarely lack candidates on paper. What they lack is time to find the right ones and confidence that the documents are real. Our job is to give them both: direct access to people and a process that checks every certificate before anyone boards. Conclusion The offshore fleet cannot grow faster than the crews who run it. DP-qualified officers, experienced anchor-handling crews and engineers who understand modern power systems will remain in demand for years. Operators that plan rotations as pipelines, build verified talent pools, measure crewing performance, grow their own officers through mentorship, onboard new people properly and look after the crews they already have will lose fewer days to late crew changes and find the right people before the gap appears, not after. About the author In 2007, a 20-year-old deck officer from Kherson looked at how seafarers found work and decided it was broken. Contracts came by fax. Agencies sat between a captain and his next ship like toll booths, each one taking a cut and adding a week. Pavel Manchenko had been on the other side of that chain, on the bridge, waiting for a call that never came on time. So he founded Marine MAN to fix it. Nineteen years later, he is still not 40, and the fix has become an ecosystem: recruitment offices in Ukraine, Georgia, India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines under one Marine MAN umbrella, connected on a single platform where AI now makes the first contact with a candidate and a human makes the decision. The numbers behind it: 200,000 seafarer profiles in the database, around 750 seafarers on board client vessels at any moment, and more than 35,000 seafarers who found their job through the platform. He holds a Master's degree from the Kyiv State Academy of Water Transport and is a certified DPA, CSO and MLC 2006 auditor, and he uses all of it: he still consults and mentors shipowners and crews on compliance, and he looks at every crew list the way an inspector would, because he has stood on the deck those inspectors walk. Then came February 2022. Marine MAN's head office and most of its core staff were in Kherson, the first regional capital in Ukraine to be occupied. Of all the crewing companies in the country, Pavel's was the first to find out what war actually means: colleagues behind the front line, phones that stopped answering, a company that had to be rebuilt piece by piece from wherever people managed to get out. Through all of it, the vessels stayed crewed and the seafarers got paid. That is not a line in a brochure; it is what Pavel's team actually did in 2022. Ask him how, and the answer is short: "Never retreat, never surrender, and keep faith in God." He has the energy of a founder half his age and the experience of one twice it. If you want to talk about how your fleet is crewed, talk to Pavel. Let's discuss cooperation. Want to know how our team can help your business?
